name: Financial Statement Analysis
blurb: How analysts read, adjust and compare IFRS and US GAAP financial statements: income statement, balance sheet, cash flows, inventories, long-lived assets, leases, taxes, reporting quality, ratios and forecasting. One of the heaviest-weighted Level I topics.
accaNote: FA/FR/SBR gave you IFRS preparation, so much of the mechanics is familiar. Focus your time on US GAAP differences (LIFO, impairment, cash-flow classification, R&D, ASC 842 operating leases), analyst adjustments, reporting-quality red flags and CFA ratio/DuPont definitions.

modules.title: Introduction to Financial Statement Analysis
modules.summary: How an analyst approaches financial statements: the analysis framework, where the information comes from (filings, notes, MD&A, auditor's report) and the role of IFRS and US GAAP.

acca.note: FA/FR gave you the statements and IFRS; AA gave you audit opinions. New for CFA: the analyst's six-step framework, US filing names (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, proxy), MD&A and the analyst's view of standard-setters vs regulators.

cards.title: Analyst, not preparer
cards.body:
ACCA trained you to **prepare** accounts. CFA asks you to **use** them: judge performance, financial position and cash-generating ability to make an investment or credit decision.

The statements are a starting point. You adjust, compare and question them, and you combine them with non-financial information (industry, competitors, economy).

cards.title: The six-step framework
cards.body:
1. **Purpose and context** (what decision? what deliverable, budget, deadline?)
2. **Collect data** (statements, notes, industry data, interviews)
3. **Process data** (adjust, common-size, ratios, forecasts)
4. **Analyse/interpret** (what do the numbers mean?)
5. **Develop and communicate conclusions** (report with recommendation)
6. **Follow-up** (update as new information arrives)

Exam favourite: ratios are computed at step 3 (*process*) but *interpreted* at step 4.

cards.title: Where information lives
rows: Accounting policies, estimates, segment data, contingencies (audited)
Management's view of results, trends, known uncertainties, critical estimates (not audited)

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body:
Terminology bridge:
- Statement of profit or loss = **income statement**
- Statement of financial position = **balance sheet**
- Statement of changes in equity = **statement of owners' equity**
- Management commentary = **MD&A** (US)

US filings: **10-K** annual, **10-Q** quarterly, **8-K** material events, **DEF 14A** proxy; foreign issuers file **20-F** (annual) and 6-K. Expect US terms in questions.

cards.title: Audit opinion types
rows: Fair except for a specific matter
Statements are materially misstated, not fair
Auditor cannot form an opinion (scope limitation)

cards.title: Key audit matters and internal control
cards.body:
Auditor reports now highlight **key audit matters** (IFRS/ISA) or **critical audit matters** (US PCAOB): areas of significant judgement, e.g. impairment or revenue estimates. Great places to start your analysis.

In the US, auditors of large public companies also opine on the effectiveness of **internal control over financial reporting** (Sarbanes-Oxley). An audit gives **reasonable assurance**, not a guarantee against fraud.

cards.title: Who sets vs who enforces
rows: SEC (US), FCA (UK), ESMA (EU coordination), IOSCO (global body of regulators)
Require and enforce reporting, review filings

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: The **conceptual framework** (IFRS) lists qualitative characteristics: fundamental = **relevance** and **faithful representation**; enhancing = comparability, verifiability, timeliness, understandability. Materiality is part of relevance. Cost is a constraint, not a characteristic.

questions.stem: An analyst calculates a set of ratios for a company and its peers. In the financial statement analysis framework, this belongs to which step?
questions.explanation: Computing ratios, common-size statements and adjustments is the **process data** step. Interpreting what the ratios mean comes next (analyse/interpret). Collecting data means gathering the statements and other inputs before any calculation.

questions.stem: Which source is most likely to contain management's discussion of known trends and uncertainties that could affect future results?
questions.explanation: MD&A (management commentary) discusses results, trends, liquidity, capital resources and known uncertainties. The auditor's report gives an opinion on fair presentation. The notes explain policies and figures but are not the place for management's forward-looking discussion.

questions.stem: Compared with the audited financial statements, information in the MD&A is best described as:
questions.explanation: MD&A is not covered by the audit opinion and includes forward-looking discussion. It is not standardised like the statements, and it is not audited for any group of filers.

questions.stem: Which statement about the financial statement analysis framework is most accurate?
options: The purpose and context of the analysis should be defined before data are collected
Follow-up is unnecessary once a recommendation is issued
Ratios should be interpreted before the data are processed
questions.explanation: Step 1 is to establish purpose and context; it drives which data you collect. Follow-up (step 6) is part of the framework, and interpretation follows processing, not the other way round.

questions.stem: An auditor concludes that, except for the treatment of inventory, the financial statements present fairly. The opinion is most likely:
questions.explanation: "Except for" language signals a **qualified** opinion. An adverse opinion says the statements as a whole are not fairly presented; a disclaimer means the auditor could not form an opinion.

questions.stem: Which organisation is a standard-setting body rather than a regulator?
questions.explanation: The FASB sets US GAAP. The SEC is the US regulator that enforces reporting, and IOSCO is an association of securities regulators.

questions.stem: An audit of financial statements provides:
options: reasonable assurance that the statements are free of material misstatement
absolute assurance that no fraud has occurred
limited assurance only on internal controls
questions.explanation: Audits give **reasonable** (high but not absolute) assurance about material misstatement. They cannot guarantee no fraud. Opinions on internal control exist for large US filers, but that is not limited assurance and is not the main purpose of the audit.

questions.stem: Under the IFRS conceptual framework, the two fundamental qualitative characteristics of useful information are:
questions.explanation: Relevance and faithful representation are fundamental. Comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability are enhancing characteristics; materiality is an aspect of relevance.

questions.stem: An analyst wants details of a company's executive compensation and board structure. The best source for a US registrant is the:
questions.explanation: The proxy statement (DEF 14A) covers executive pay, board members and matters for shareholder vote. The 10-Q is the quarterly report; the 8-K reports material events.

questions.stem: Which information is least likely to be covered by the auditor's opinion?
options: Management's commentary on future capital spending
questions.explanation: Management commentary/MD&A is outside the audited statements. The notes (including segment disclosures) and the cash flow statement are part of the audited financial statements.

questions.stem: An auditor is unable to obtain sufficient evidence about a material subsidiary and cannot form an opinion. The report will contain:
options: an unqualified opinion with a key audit matter
questions.explanation: A scope limitation so severe that no opinion can be formed results in a **disclaimer**. An adverse opinion requires the auditor to conclude the statements are materially misstated. A key audit matter does not change a clean opinion.

questions.stem: In the financial statement analysis framework, an analyst revisits her credit recommendation after the company releases quarterly results. This activity is part of:
questions.explanation: Periodically updating analysis as new information arrives is **follow-up** (step 6). Processing data is computing adjustments and ratios; communicating conclusions is issuing the report.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a role of the SEC rather than the FASB?
options: Developing the conceptual framework for US GAAP
questions.explanation: The SEC is the regulator that mandates filings such as the 10-K. Issuing ASUs and developing the conceptual framework are FASB (standard-setter) roles.

flashcards.front: Six steps of the FSA framework
flashcards.back: Purpose/context → collect data → process data → analyse/interpret → develop and communicate conclusions → follow-up.
10-K = annual report; 10-Q = quarterly report; 8-K = material event (M&A, auditor change, CEO exit). 20-F = annual report of a foreign private issuer.
Unqualified (clean), qualified ("except for"), adverse (not fair), disclaimer (cannot form opinion).
Standard-setters (IASB, FASB) write standards. Regulators (SEC, FCA, ESMA; IOSCO as their global body) have legal power to require and enforce reporting.
Relevance (incl. materiality) and faithful representation. Enhancing: comparability, verifiability, timeliness, understandability.
No. MD&A/management commentary is outside the audit opinion, so treat it with more scepticism than the notes.

modules.title: Analyzing Income Statements
modules.summary: Revenue and expense recognition, non-recurring items and accounting changes, EPS (basic and diluted), and how analysts read the income statement.

acca.note: IFRS 15, IAS 8 and IAS 33 EPS are core FR/SBR. New for CFA: US GAAP terms (discontinued ops, unusual or infrequent items), analyst treatment of non-recurring items, and heavy testing of diluted EPS with the treasury stock method and antidilution.

cards.title: Five-step model (IFRS 15 = ASC 606)
cards.body:
IFRS and US GAAP are converged on revenue:
1. Identify the contract
2. Identify performance obligations
3. Determine the transaction price
4. Allocate price to obligations
5. Recognise revenue when (or as) each obligation is satisfied

Over time (e.g. construction) uses progress, typically cost incurred ÷ total expected cost.

cards.title: Progress-based revenue
cards.body:
Contract price 10.0m; total expected cost 8.0m; cost incurred in year 1 is 2.0m.

Progress = 2.0/8.0 = 25%
Revenue = 25% × 10.0m = **2.5m**; profit = 2.5 − 2.0 = **0.5m**.

If the outcome were expected to be a loss, the whole expected loss is recognised immediately.

cards.title: Expense recognition and analyst choices
cards.body:
Matching: costs follow the revenue they help earn (COGS). Period costs (admin) are expensed as incurred.

Analyst focus areas are the **estimates**: bad-debt allowance, warranty provisions, useful lives, inventory method. A company that lengthens asset lives or cuts its doubtful-debt allowance boosts profit without better operations.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: US GAAP income statements often show **COGS** and **SG&A**, and many US companies present **by function**. IFRS allows **by nature** (raw materials, staff costs, depreciation) or by function. CFA labels: "net revenue" = revenue after returns and allowances; "gross profit" = revenue − COGS; "operating income" ≈ EBIT for non-financial firms.

cards.title: Discontinued operations
cards.body:
A component that has been disposed of or is held for sale, physically and operationally distinguishable. Shown **separately, net of tax, below income from continuing operations** under both IFRS and US GAAP.

Analysts usually exclude it when forecasting, because it will not recur.

cards.title: Unusual items: IFRS vs US GAAP
rows: Shown in continuing ops (pre-tax), often separate line

cards.title: Accounting changes
rows: Change in accounting policy (e.g. FIFO → weighted average)
Change in estimate (useful life, bad debts)
Prospective: current and future periods only

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: Same IAS 8 logic you learned. CFA adds two things: (1) US GAAP exception, a change in **depreciation method** is treated as a change in estimate (prospective); (2) the analyst angle, frequent restatements or repeated "non-recurring" charges are a reporting-quality warning sign.

cards.title: Basic EPS
cards.note: Stock splits and stock dividends are applied retroactively to all periods, as if they happened at the start.

cards.title: Diluted EPS
cards.formula: Diluted EPS = [NI − pref div + conv. pref div + conv. debt interest × (1 − t)] ÷ [WASO + conversion shares + TSM shares]
where: average market price for the period
cards.note: Options dilute only if P̄ > X. Exclude any antidilutive security (one that raises EPS).

cards.title: Treasury stock method
cards.body:
10,000 options, exercise price $20, average price $25.

Proceeds = 10,000 × 20 = $200,000 → buy back 200,000 ÷ 25 = 8,000 shares.
New shares = 10,000 − 8,000 = **2,000**.

Under US GAAP and IFRS the same TSM logic applies; the denominator rises, the numerator does not change.

cards.title: Convertible bond
cards.body:
NI $1.2m, 500,000 shares, 6% convertible bonds of $1m convertible into 50,000 shares, tax 30%.

Basic = 1.2m ÷ 500,000 = $2.40
Add back after-tax interest: 60,000 × 0.7 = 42,000
Diluted = 1,242,000 ÷ 550,000 = **$2.26**

Check: incremental EPS = 42,000 ÷ 50,000 = 0.84 < 2.40, so dilutive.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body:
- Forgetting **(1 − t)** on convertible debt interest.
- Not time-weighting shares issued during the year (shares issued April 1 count 9/12).
- Including options when the average price is **below** the exercise price.
- For convertible preferred, add back the preferred dividend (no tax adjustment).

questions.stem: A builder has a fixed-price contract of $20 million with total expected costs of $16 million. Costs incurred in year 1 are $6 million. Using cost-based progress, year 1 revenue is closest to:
questions.explanation: Progress = 6/16 = 37.5%; revenue = 37.5% × 20 = **$7.5 million**. $6.0m confuses revenue with cost incurred; $4.0m is total expected profit, not revenue.

questions.stem: Under the five-step model, which step comes immediately after identifying the performance obligations?
options: Allocate the price to performance obligations
questions.explanation: The order is contract → performance obligations → transaction price → allocate → recognise.

questions.stem: A company lengthens the estimated useful life of its machinery. All else equal, in the current year this will most likely:
options: have no effect on net income
questions.explanation: A longer life lowers annual depreciation, raising net income. It has no cash effect, which is why analysts watch for such estimate changes.

questions.stem: Under both IFRS and US GAAP, if a long-term contract is expected to make an overall loss, the loss is:
options: spread over the contract by progress
questions.explanation: Expected contract losses are recognised immediately in full (prudence/onerous contract). Spreading or deferring would overstate interim profits.

questions.stem: A company changes its inventory cost formula from FIFO to weighted average. This is most likely applied:
options: only in the notes with no restatement
questions.explanation: A change in accounting policy is applied **retrospectively**, restating prior periods for comparability. Prospective application is for changes in estimate.

questions.stem: Under US GAAP, a change in depreciation method is accounted for as:
options: a change in estimate, applied prospectively
a change in accounting policy, applied retrospectively
questions.explanation: US GAAP treats a change in depreciation method as a change in estimate effected by a change in principle, applied **prospectively**.

questions.stem: Income from discontinued operations is reported:
options: as an extraordinary item under IFRS
net of tax, after income from continuing operations
questions.explanation: Discontinued operations appear net of tax below continuing operations. Extraordinary items are prohibited under IFRS and no longer exist under US GAAP.

questions.stem: A company has reported a "restructuring charge" in each of the last five years. An analyst should most likely:
options: treat the charges as a recurring cost of operations
questions.explanation: Charges that occur every year are effectively recurring; excluding them overstates sustainable earnings. They do not meet the definition of discontinued operations.

questions.stem: A company has net income of $5,000,000 and pays preferred dividends of $500,000. It had 1,000,000 common shares on 1 January and issued 200,000 shares on 1 April. Basic EPS is closest to:
questions.explanation: WASO = 1,000,000 + 200,000 × 9/12 = 1,150,000. Basic EPS = (5,000,000 − 500,000) ÷ 1,150,000 = **$3.91**. $3.75 ignores time-weighting (1,200,000 shares). $4.35 forgets to deduct preferred dividends.

questions.stem: A firm had 100,000 shares on 1 January, issued 20,000 shares on 1 July and declared a 2-for-1 stock split on 1 October. Weighted-average shares for EPS are:
questions.explanation: Splits are applied retroactively: (100,000 + 20,000 × 6/12) × 2 = **220,000**. 240,000 ignores time-weighting; 210,000 applies the split only to the opening shares.

questions.stem: Net income is $1,000,000, preferred dividends are $200,000 and WASO is 200,000. The preferred shares are convertible into 40,000 common shares. Diluted EPS is:
questions.explanation: Basic EPS = 800,000 ÷ 200,000 = $4.00. If converted: 1,000,000 ÷ 240,000 = $4.17, which is **higher** than basic, so the preferred is antidilutive and excluded. Diluted EPS = **$4.00**. $5.00 is the incremental EPS of the preferred (200,000 ÷ 40,000).

questions.stem: Options with an exercise price of $50 are outstanding. The average share price for the year was $45. For diluted EPS, the options:
options: add shares using the treasury stock method
are included at their full number of shares
questions.explanation: When the average price is below the exercise price the options are out-of-the-money; the TSM would produce negative incremental shares, so they are antidilutive and excluded.

questions.stem: Net income is $2,000,000; non-convertible preferred dividends are $100,000; WASO is 1,000,000. There are 100,000 options with an exercise price of $30 (average share price $40), and $2,000,000 of 5% convertible bonds convertible into 60,000 shares. The tax rate is 25%. Diluted EPS is closest to:
questions.explanation: Basic = 1,900,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = $1.90. TSM shares = 100,000 − 3,000,000 ÷ 40 = 25,000. Bond add-back = 100,000 × 0.75 = 75,000 for 60,000 shares (1.25 per share < 1.90, dilutive). Diluted = 1,975,000 ÷ 1,085,000 = **$1.82**. $1.85 includes only the options; $1.70 adds all 100,000 option shares instead of the TSM net shares.

questions.stem: Which of the following would an analyst most likely exclude when forecasting a company's sustainable earnings?
questions.explanation: Discontinued operations will not continue, so they are excluded from forecasts. Recurring restructuring charges and COGS are part of ongoing operations.

questions.stem: A company discovers that last year's depreciation was understated because of a calculation error. The correction is most likely reported:
options: prospectively in the current year's depreciation
as an unusual item in current-year income
questions.explanation: Prior-period errors are corrected **retrospectively** by restating comparatives (IAS 8 and ASC 250). Prospective treatment is for changes in estimate.

questions.stem: A company has convertible bonds whose after-tax interest is $90,000 and which convert into 30,000 shares. Basic EPS is $2.50. The bonds are:
options: dilutive, because the incremental EPS of $3.00 exceeds basic EPS
antidilutive, because the incremental EPS of $3.00 exceeds basic EPS
questions.explanation: Incremental EPS = 90,000 ÷ 30,000 = $3.00. Since $3.00 > basic $2.50, including the bonds would raise EPS, so they are **antidilutive** and excluded. Adding shares alone does not make a security dilutive.

questions.stem: Under IFRS, which presentation of expenses on the income statement is permitted?
options: Either by nature or by function
questions.explanation: IFRS permits classification by nature (e.g. staff costs, depreciation) or by function (e.g. COGS, distribution, admin), with by-nature disclosures if function is used. US GAAP practice is mainly by function for SEC filers.

flashcards.back: (NI − preferred dividends) ÷ weighted-average common shares. Splits and stock dividends restated retroactively.
n − (n × X) ÷ P̄. Only if average price P̄ > exercise price X.
Add back interest × (1 − t) to numerator; add conversion shares to denominator.
Incremental EPS of a security = numerator add-back ÷ added shares. If > basic EPS, exclude it.

flashcards.front: Change in policy vs estimate vs error
flashcards.back: Policy → retrospective. Estimate → prospective. Error → retrospective restatement. (US GAAP: depreciation method change = estimate, prospective.)
Separate line, net of tax, below income from continuing operations (IFRS and US GAAP).
Prohibited under IFRS; eliminated from US GAAP. US GAAP shows unusual or infrequent items within continuing ops, pre-tax.

modules.title: Analyzing Balance Sheets
modules.summary: Classification and measurement of assets and liabilities, intangibles and goodwill, financial instruments, and common-size and ratio analysis of the balance sheet.

acca.note: Statement of financial position, goodwill, IFRS 9 categories and current/non-current classification are FR/SBR material. New for CFA: US GAAP categories and terminology, and the analyst ratios (quick, cash, D/E, financial leverage) applied to common-size balance sheets.

cards.title: Measurement bases
cards.body:
Balance sheets mix measurement bases: historical cost (PP&E, inventory), amortised cost (loans, held-to-maturity bonds), fair value (trading securities, derivatives), and NRV/lower-of tests.

So book equity is **not** a measure of market value. Analysts adjust where it matters, e.g. adding back LIFO reserve or valuing off-balance-sheet items.

cards.title: Financial assets: IFRS 9 vs US GAAP
Goodwill and intangibles
cards.body:
**Goodwill** = purchase price − fair value of identifiable net assets acquired. Only acquired goodwill is recognised; internally generated goodwill is never capitalised.

Goodwill is **not amortised** under IFRS or US GAAP (public companies); it is tested for impairment at least annually.

Example: pay 500 for net assets with FV 380 → goodwill **120**.

Analysts often exclude goodwill when computing tangible book value.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: Same IFRS logic, different labels. US GAAP calls a classified balance sheet's liabilities "current" and "long-term"; IFRS uses "non-current". US GAAP lists the most liquid assets **first**; many IFRS reporters list non-current assets first. Under US GAAP, unrealised gains on equity investments go to **net income** (no FVOCI election for equities).

cards.title: Common-size balance sheet
cards.body:
Express every line as a **% of total assets**. This removes size and lets you compare firms and years.

What to look for: rising receivables or inventory share (collection or obsolescence issues), falling cash, rising debt share, large goodwill relative to equity.

cards.title: Liquidity ratios
cards.formula:
Current = CA ÷ CL
Quick = (cash + ST marketable securities + receivables) ÷ CL
Cash = (cash + ST marketable securities) ÷ CL
cards.note: Quick excludes inventory and prepaid expenses because they are less liquid.

cards.title: Solvency ratios
cards.formula:
D/E = total debt ÷ total equity
D/A = total debt ÷ total assets
D/capital = debt ÷ (debt + equity)
Financial leverage = avg total assets ÷ avg total equity

cards.title: Liquidity example
cards.body:
Cash 50, marketable securities 30, receivables 120, inventory 200, prepaid 20; current liabilities 250.

Current = 420 ÷ 250 = **1.68**
Quick = 200 ÷ 250 = **0.80**
Cash = 80 ÷ 250 = **0.32**

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: ACCA's "acid test" = CFA's **quick ratio**. ACCA "gearing" is usually debt ÷ (debt + equity) = CFA's **debt-to-capital**. CFA also uses **financial leverage** (assets ÷ equity), the DuPont leverage term. Check which definition the question uses.

questions.stem: Under IFRS 9, unrealised gains on a debt security classified at fair value through OCI are reported in:
options: neither, as the security is held at amortised cost
questions.explanation: FVOCI unrealised gains/losses go to **OCI** (recycled to P&L on sale for debt). FVPL gains go to profit or loss; amortised cost assets are not remeasured.

questions.stem: A company pays $500 million for a target whose identifiable net assets have a fair value of $380 million and a book value of $300 million. Goodwill is:
questions.explanation: Goodwill = price − **fair value** of identifiable net assets = 500 − 380 = **$120m**. $200m wrongly uses book value; $80m is the fair value uplift on net assets.

questions.stem: Under both IFRS and US GAAP (public companies), goodwill is:
options: amortised over its useful life up to 40 years
not amortised but tested for impairment at least annually
questions.explanation: Goodwill has an indefinite life; it is not amortised but tested for impairment at least annually.

questions.stem: A US company holds equity shares of another firm (no significant influence). Changes in their fair value are generally reported in:
options: neither, as they are carried at cost
questions.explanation: Under US GAAP, equity investments without significant influence are measured at fair value through **net income**. IFRS allows an irrevocable FVOCI election for equities, but US GAAP does not.

questions.stem: A company reports cash $50, marketable securities $30, receivables $120, inventory $200, prepaid expenses $20 and current liabilities $250. Its quick ratio is closest to:
questions.explanation: Quick = (50 + 30 + 120) ÷ 250 = **0.80**. 1.68 is the current ratio (all current assets of 420); 1.60 excludes only the prepaid expenses (400 ÷ 250).

questions.stem: A company has total debt of $400 and total equity of $600. Its debt-to-capital ratio is:
questions.explanation: Debt-to-capital = 400 ÷ (400 + 600) = **0.40**. 0.67 is debt-to-equity; 1.50 is equity-to-debt.

questions.stem: In a common-size balance sheet, each item is expressed as a percentage of:
questions.explanation: Vertical common-size balance sheets divide by **total assets**. Revenue is the base for the common-size income statement.

questions.stem: A company uses cash to pay down a short-term payable. If its current ratio was 1.5 before the payment, the current ratio will most likely:
questions.explanation: Equal reductions in CA and CL raise a ratio above 1. E.g. 150/100 → 140/90 = 1.56. If the ratio were below 1 it would fall.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely excluded from the quick ratio?
questions.explanation: The quick ratio excludes inventory (and prepaid expenses) because they are less readily converted to cash. Receivables and marketable securities are included.

questions.stem: A company's average total assets are $5,000 and average total equity is $2,000. Its financial leverage ratio and debt-to-assets ratio (assuming all liabilities are debt) are closest to:
questions.explanation: Financial leverage = 5,000 ÷ 2,000 = **2.5**. Liabilities = 5,000 − 2,000 = 3,000, so D/A = 3,000 ÷ 5,000 = **0.60**. 0.40 is equity ÷ assets.

questions.stem: Under IFRS 9, a debt instrument held in a business model whose objective is solely to collect contractual cash flows of principal and interest is measured at:
options: fair value through profit or loss
questions.explanation: Hold-to-collect plus SPPI cash flows → **amortised cost**. Hold-to-collect-and-sell → FVOCI; anything else → FVPL.

questions.stem: An analyst computing tangible book value per share would most likely:
options: subtract goodwill and other intangibles from equity
subtract deferred tax liabilities from equity
questions.explanation: Tangible book value removes goodwill (and usually other intangibles) because they may have little realisable value in liquidation.

questions.stem: Company X's common-size balance sheet shows receivables rising from 12% to 19% of total assets over two years while revenue is flat. The most likely concern is:
options: deteriorating collection or aggressive revenue recognition
questions.explanation: Receivables growing much faster than revenue suggests slower collection or revenue booked before cash is likely, a classic warning sign. It does not mean better liquidity, and it says nothing about leverage directly.

flashcards.back: Current = CA/CL. Quick = (cash + ST securities + receivables)/CL. Cash = (cash + ST securities)/CL.
Price paid − FV of identifiable net assets. Not amortised; impairment test at least annually. Internally generated goodwill never recognised.

flashcards.front: IFRS 9 categories → US GAAP debt categories
flashcards.back: Amortised cost ↔ held-to-maturity; FVOCI ↔ available-for-sale; FVPL ↔ trading.

flashcards.front: Equity investments: US GAAP vs IFRS
flashcards.back: US GAAP: fair value through net income. IFRS: FVPL, or irrevocable FVOCI election (no recycling).
Average total assets ÷ average total equity (the DuPont equity multiplier).
Total assets.

modules.title: Analyzing Statements of Cash Flows I
modules.summary: How the cash flow statement links to the income statement and balance sheet, the direct and indirect methods, converting indirect to direct, and IFRS vs US GAAP classification.

acca.note: IAS 7 and the indirect method are FA/FR staples. New for CFA: US GAAP's fixed classification of interest and dividends, converting an indirect statement to the direct method line by line, and CFO/CFI/CFF terminology.

cards.title: Three activities
cards.body:
- **CFO** (operating): cash from the core business: customers, suppliers, employees, taxes.
- **CFI** (investing): buying/selling long-term assets and investments not held for trading.
- **CFF** (financing): borrowing and repaying debt, issuing/buying back shares, paying dividends (US GAAP).

Non-cash investing/financing (e.g. converting debt to equity, acquiring an asset with a lease) is disclosed in a note, not in the statement.

cards.title: Reclassifying IFRS to US GAAP
cards.body:
An IFRS reporter shows CFO of 500. It classified interest paid of 40 in CFF and dividends received of 15 in CFI.

US GAAP basis: interest paid must be in CFO (−40) and dividends received in CFO (+15).
CFO = 500 − 40 + 15 = **475**.

Analysts make this adjustment to compare an IFRS firm with a US peer.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body:
Heads-up: IFRS 18 (effective for periods from 1 January 2027) removes most of these choices for ordinary companies. The CFA curriculum tables still test the IAS 7 choices shown here, so answer exam questions with the choices.

Why it matters: an IFRS firm putting interest paid in CFF shows a **higher CFO** than an identical US GAAP firm.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: Same IAS 7 you know, new shorthand: **CFO / CFI / CFF**. Big difference: US GAAP has **no choice** for interest and dividends. Memory hook: US GAAP puts everything that hits net income (interest paid, interest and dividends received) in CFO; dividends paid don't hit NI, so CFF.

cards.title: Indirect CFO
cards.formula: CFO = NI + non-cash charges − gains + losses − Δ operating current assets + Δ operating current liabilities
where: depreciation, amortisation, impairment, deferred tax expense
on sale of long-term assets (proceeds go to CFI)
cards.note: Increase in an asset = use of cash (subtract); increase in a liability = source of cash (add).

cards.title: Indirect CFO example
cards.body:
NI 800; depreciation 150; gain on sale of equipment 40; receivables up 60; inventory down 30; payables up 25; wages payable down 10.

CFO = 800 + 150 − 40 − 60 + 30 + 25 − 10 = **895**.

cards.title: Cash from selling PP&E
cards.body:
Gross PP&E: beginning 1,000, end 1,100, purchases 300. Accumulated depreciation: beginning 400, end 420, depreciation expense 100. Gain on sale 30.

Cost of asset sold = 1,000 + 300 − 1,100 = 200
Acc. dep. on asset sold = 400 + 100 − 420 = 80
Book value sold = 120
Proceeds (CFI inflow) = 120 + 30 = **150**

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: The **gain** on sale is subtracted in CFO because the full proceeds appear in CFI. Leaving it in double counts. Also: changes in **short-term debt** and **dividends payable** are financing, not operating working capital.

lessons.title: Direct method and converting indirect to direct

cards.title: Why the direct method matters
cards.body:
The direct method shows actual operating cash receipts and payments (from customers, to suppliers, to employees). It is more informative for forecasting, but most companies use the indirect method.

IFRS and US GAAP both encourage the direct method; US GAAP then requires a reconciliation of NI to CFO (i.e. the indirect method) in the notes.

cards.title: Converting income statement lines to cash
cards.formula:
Cash from customers = revenue − ΔAR + Δunearned revenue
Cash to suppliers = COGS + Δinventory − ΔAP
Cash to employees = salary expense − Δsalaries payable
Cash interest = interest expense − Δinterest payable
Cash taxes = tax expense − Δtaxes payable − ΔDTL + ΔDTA
cards.note: Sign logic: asset up = less cash in/more cash out; liability up = more cash kept.

cards.title: Direct-method lines
cards.body:
Revenue 5,000; AR up 200; unearned revenue up 50 → cash from customers = 5,000 − 200 + 50 = **4,850**.

COGS 3,000; inventory up 150; AP up 100 → cash to suppliers = 3,000 + 150 − 100 = **3,050**.

Tax expense 400; taxes payable down 30 → cash taxes = **430**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Never include depreciation, amortisation, gains or losses in direct-method CFO: they are non-cash or belong in CFI. Payments to suppliers are an **outflow**; questions usually ask for the positive amount paid.

questions.stem: Under US GAAP, dividends paid to shareholders are classified as:
questions.explanation: US GAAP requires dividends paid in **CFF**. Under IFRS they may be CFO or CFF. They are never investing.

questions.stem: Under US GAAP, interest received on a bond investment is classified as:
questions.explanation: US GAAP: interest and dividends received are **CFO**. The CFO-or-CFI choice exists only under IFRS.

questions.stem: An IFRS company reports CFO of $500. It classifies interest paid of $40 as financing and dividends received of $15 as investing. CFO restated to a US GAAP basis is closest to:
questions.explanation: Move interest paid into CFO (−40) and dividends received into CFO (+15): 500 − 40 + 15 = **$475**. $525 reverses the signs; $555 adds both items.

questions.stem: A company acquires a building by issuing common shares directly to the seller. In the statement of cash flows this transaction is:
options: disclosed as a non-cash investing and financing activity
questions.explanation: No cash changed hands, so it is excluded from the statement and **disclosed** as a significant non-cash investing and financing activity.

questions.stem: Net income is $800, depreciation $150, gain on sale of equipment $40; receivables increased $60, inventory decreased $30, accounts payable increased $25 and wages payable decreased $10. CFO is:
questions.explanation: CFO = 800 + 150 − 40 − 60 + 30 + 25 − 10 = **$895**. $975 adds the gain instead of subtracting it. $925 reverses every working-capital sign.

questions.stem: Using the indirect method, an increase in accounts receivable is:
questions.explanation: Higher receivables mean revenue was recognised but not yet collected; subtract the increase.

questions.stem: Gross PP&E rose from $1,000 to $1,100 after purchases of $300. Accumulated depreciation rose from $400 to $420 with depreciation expense of $100. The equipment sold produced a gain of $30. Cash proceeds from the sale were:
questions.explanation: Cost sold = 1,000 + 300 − 1,100 = 200; acc. dep. sold = 400 + 100 − 420 = 80; BV = 120; proceeds = 120 + 30 = **$150**. $120 is the book value; $230 adds the gain to the cost.

questions.stem: Which item is added back to net income when computing CFO by the indirect method?
questions.explanation: An increase in DTL means tax expense exceeded taxes paid, a non-cash charge, so it is added back. Gains are subtracted; an inventory increase uses cash.

questions.stem: Revenue is $5,000. Accounts receivable increased by $200 and unearned revenue increased by $50. Cash collected from customers is:
questions.explanation: Cash from customers = 5,000 − 200 + 50 = **$4,850**. $5,250 adds the AR increase; $4,750 subtracts the unearned revenue increase, which is actually cash received in advance.

questions.stem: COGS is $3,000, inventory increased by $150 and accounts payable increased by $100. Cash paid to suppliers is:
questions.explanation: Cash to suppliers = COGS + Δinventory − ΔAP = 3,000 + 150 − 100 = **$3,050**. $2,950 reverses both signs; $3,250 adds the AP increase.

questions.stem: Salary expense is $1,200 and salaries payable decreased by $20 during the year. Cash paid to employees is:
questions.explanation: A fall in salaries payable means the company paid more than the expense: 1,200 + 20 = **$1,220**.

questions.stem: Under US GAAP, a company that presents CFO using the direct method must also:
options: provide a reconciliation of net income to CFO
present CFI using the indirect method
questions.explanation: US GAAP requires the NI-to-CFO reconciliation (indirect) when the direct method is used. CFI has no indirect method, and US GAAP classifies interest paid in CFO.

questions.stem: An IFRS company reports CFO of $1,200. It classified interest paid of $60 and dividends paid of $90 in CFO, and interest received of $20 in CFI. On a US GAAP basis, CFO is closest to:
questions.explanation: US GAAP puts dividends paid in CFF, so remove that outflow from CFO (+90); interest paid stays in CFO; interest received moves into CFO (+20). CFO = 1,200 + 90 + 20 = **$1,310**. $1,220 moves only interest received; $1,370 also removes interest paid from CFO, which US GAAP does not allow.

questions.stem: Which change in a balance sheet account is a source of operating cash in the indirect method?
questions.explanation: An increase in an operating liability means expenses were recognised but not paid, so it is added back (a source). An increase in prepaids and a decrease in payables both use cash.

questions.stem: Tax expense is $400, taxes payable decreased by $30 and the deferred tax liability increased by $20. Cash taxes paid are closest to:
questions.explanation: Cash taxes = 400 + 30 (payable fell, so extra cash paid) − 20 (DTL rose, so part of the expense is deferred) = **$410**. $450 adds the DTL increase instead of subtracting it; $390 reverses both adjustments.

questions.stem: Which statement about the indirect method is most accurate?
options: It reports cash receipts from customers directly
It starts with net income and adjusts for non-cash items and working-capital changes
questions.explanation: The indirect method reconciles net income to CFO. The direct method shows receipts from customers. Both methods are permitted under IFRS and US GAAP.

questions.stem: A company sold equipment with an original cost of $200 and accumulated depreciation of $80 for $100 cash. In an indirect-method cash flow statement:
options: CFO subtracts a $20 gain and CFI shows a $120 inflow
CFO adds back a $20 loss and CFI shows a $100 inflow
CFO is unaffected and CFI shows a $100 inflow
questions.explanation: BV = 200 − 80 = 120; proceeds 100 → loss of 20. The loss is **added back** in CFO (it reduced NI but used no cash), and the $100 proceeds appear in CFI.

flashcards.front: Interest paid: IFRS vs US GAAP
flashcards.back: IFRS: CFO or CFF. US GAAP: CFO.

flashcards.front: Dividends paid: IFRS vs US GAAP
flashcards.back: IFRS: CFO or CFF. US GAAP: CFF.

flashcards.front: Interest and dividends received: IFRS vs US GAAP
flashcards.back: IFRS: CFO or CFI. US GAAP: CFO.
Revenue − ΔAR + Δunearned revenue.
COGS + Δinventory − ΔAP.
Tax expense − Δtaxes payable − ΔDTL + ΔDTA.
Operating asset ↑ → subtract. Operating liability ↑ → add. Gains subtract, losses add, non-cash charges add.
Excluded from the CFS; disclosed in a note or supplementary schedule.

modules.title: Analyzing Statements of Cash Flows II
modules.summary: Reading and common-sizing the cash flow statement, computing free cash flow to the firm and to equity, and cash-flow performance and coverage ratios.

acca.note: FR covered cash flow interpretation and FM free cash flow ideas. New for CFA: the exact FCFF and FCFE formulas starting from CFO, common-size cash flow statements, and the named cash-flow ratios.

cards.title: Reading the CFS
cards.body:
Ask: what are the **major sources and uses** of cash? Is CFO driven by profits or by squeezing working capital? Is capex covering depreciation (replacing the asset base)? Is the company funding dividends with debt?

A healthy mature firm: positive CFO funding capex and dividends. A growth firm: negative CFI funded by CFF. Warning: positive NI but negative CFO for several years.

cards.title: Free cash flow
cards.formula:
FCFF = CFO + Int × (1 − t) − FCInv
FCFE = CFO − FCInv + net borrowing
where: capital expenditure net of proceeds from asset sales
interest paid (in CFO under US GAAP)
cards.note: Add back after-tax interest only if interest paid was deducted in CFO.

cards.title: FCFF and FCFE
cards.body:
CFO 1,000; interest paid 100; tax rate 25%; net capex 400; net borrowing 150.

FCFF = 1,000 + 100 × 0.75 − 400 = **675**
FCFE = 1,000 − 400 + 150 = **750**

Check: FCFE = FCFF − Int(1 − t) + net borrowing = 675 − 75 + 150 = 750.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: FM taught "free cash flow" loosely. CFA is precise: **FCFF** belongs to all capital providers (discount at WACC); **FCFE** belongs to shareholders after debt flows (discount at cost of equity). These reappear in Equities and Corporate Finance.

cards.title: Common-size cash flow statement
cards.body:
Two approaches:
1. Each line as a **% of revenue**: shows how much cash each sales dollar generates.
2. Each inflow as a % of **total inflows** and each outflow as a % of **total outflows**: shows the mix of sources and uses.

cards.title: Coverage ratios
rows: (CFO + interest paid + taxes paid) ÷ interest paid
CFO ÷ cash paid for long-term assets
CFO ÷ cash outflows for investing and financing

cards.title: Ratio example
cards.body:
CFO 600; interest paid 50; taxes paid 150; capex 400; avg total assets 4,000.

Cash interest coverage = (600 + 50 + 150) ÷ 50 = **16.0×**
Reinvestment = 600 ÷ 400 = **1.5×**
Cash ROA = 600 ÷ 4,000 = **15%**

questions.stem: CFO is $2,400, net capital expenditure is $800, interest paid is $200 and the tax rate is 30%. FCFF is closest to:
questions.explanation: FCFF = 2,400 + 200 × 0.7 − 800 = **$1,740**. $1,800 adds back pre-tax interest; $1,600 forgets to add back interest at all.

questions.stem: Using the same company (CFO $2,400, net capex $800), it issued $500 of new debt and repaid $300. FCFE is closest to:
questions.explanation: FCFE = 2,400 − 800 + (500 − 300) = **$1,800**. $2,100 uses gross borrowing of 500; $1,660 deducts after-tax interest, which is already in CFO.

questions.stem: Free cash flow to the firm is the cash flow available to:
options: all providers of capital (debt and equity)
questions.explanation: FCFF is before payments to debt holders, so it belongs to all capital providers. FCFE is after debt flows and belongs to equity holders.

questions.stem: A company has reported positive and growing net income for three years while CFO has been negative and falling. This most likely indicates:
options: earnings driven by accruals such as growing receivables
questions.explanation: Persistent gaps between NI and CFO indicate earnings built on accruals (e.g. rising receivables or inventory), a warning sign for earnings quality.

questions.stem: CFO is $600, interest paid is $50 and taxes paid are $150. The cash interest coverage ratio is:
questions.explanation: (600 + 50 + 150) ÷ 50 = **16.0**. 12.0 uses CFO alone; 13.0 adds back interest but not taxes.

questions.stem: A reinvestment ratio above 1.0 indicates that:
options: the company is reinvesting more than its earnings
CFO is sufficient to fund purchases of long-term assets
questions.explanation: Reinvestment = CFO ÷ cash paid for long-term assets. Above 1.0 means operating cash covers capex.

questions.stem: In a common-size cash flow statement using the total-inflows/total-outflows approach, each outflow is expressed as a percentage of:
questions.explanation: Under that approach, inflows are scaled by total inflows and outflows by total outflows. The alternative approach scales by revenue.

questions.stem: CFO is $600 and average total assets are $4,000. Cash return on assets is:

A US GAAP company reports CFO of $900, capital expenditures of $350, proceeds from sale of equipment of $50, interest paid of $80, dividends paid of $120, net debt repayment of $100 and a tax rate of 25%. FCFE is closest to:
questions.explanation: Net FCInv = 350 − 50 = 300. FCFE = 900 − 300 − 100 = **$500**. Dividends are a use of FCFE, not a deduction from it ($380 deducts them). $560 adds back after-tax interest, which belongs only in FCFF.

questions.stem: Using the same data (CFO $900, net FCInv $300, interest paid $80, tax rate 25%), FCFF is closest to:
questions.explanation: FCFF = 900 + 80 × 0.75 − 300 = **$660**. $680 adds back pre-tax interest; $600 omits the interest add-back.

questions.stem: Which ratio best indicates a company's ability to pay dividends from operating cash flow?
questions.explanation: The dividend payment ratio is CFO ÷ dividends paid. Dividends ÷ NI is the payout ratio (accrual based); CFO ÷ total debt is debt coverage.

questions.stem: A company's CFO is consistently lower than capital expenditure and it funds the gap with new borrowing each year. An analyst should most likely conclude that:
options: the company has strong cash generation
FCFE is negative before net borrowing and growth depends on external financing
questions.explanation: CFO below capex means FCF before borrowing is negative, so the firm relies on external capital. That is not strong cash generation, and FCFF exceeds CFO only if after-tax interest exceeds net capex, which is not the case here.

questions.stem: Company A and B have identical CFO. A is an IFRS reporter that classifies interest paid in CFF; B is a US GAAP reporter. Compared with B, A's reported CFO is most likely:
options: higher, because interest paid is excluded from CFO
lower, because interest paid is included in CFO
the same, because interest classification is identical
questions.explanation: If A classifies interest paid as financing, its CFO excludes that outflow and is higher than a comparable US GAAP firm, which must deduct interest in CFO. Analysts reclassify before comparing.

flashcards.back: FCFF = CFO + Int(1 − t) − FCInv.
FCFE = CFO − FCInv + net borrowing (debt issued − repaid).
FCFE = FCFF − Int(1 − t) + net borrowing.
(CFO + interest paid + taxes paid) ÷ interest paid.
CFO ÷ cash paid for long-term assets.

flashcards.front: Two ways to common-size a CFS
flashcards.back: (1) Each line ÷ revenue; (2) inflows ÷ total inflows and outflows ÷ total outflows.

modules.title: Analysis of Inventories
modules.summary: Inventory cost formulas including LIFO (US GAAP only), the LIFO reserve and LIFO-to-FIFO adjustments, write-downs and reversals, and the effect of methods on ratios.

acca.note: IAS 2 (FIFO, weighted average, NRV write-downs) is FA/FR. Entirely new: LIFO, the LIFO reserve and LIFO liquidation, US GAAP lower-of-cost-or-market, the no-reversal rule under US GAAP, and analyst conversions from LIFO to FIFO.

lessons.title: Cost formulas: FIFO, weighted average, LIFO

cards.title: Permitted methods
rows: Permitted (LIFO conformity: if used for tax, must use for books)

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: LIFO was banned under IAS 2, so you never practised it. Key intuition: in inflation LIFO gives the most **economically realistic income statement** (current costs in COGS) while FIFO gives the most **realistic balance sheet** (inventory at recent costs). Weighted average sits in between. In deflation, all directions flip.

cards.title: LIFO to FIFO
cards.formula:
Inv_{FIFO} = Inv_{LIFO} + LIFO reserve
COGS_{FIFO} = COGS_{LIFO} − ΔLIFO reserve
NI_{FIFO} = NI_{LIFO} + ΔLIFO reserve × (1 − t)
where: FIFO inventory − LIFO inventory (disclosed by US LIFO firms)
cards.note: Balance sheet: equity (retained earnings) rises by reserve × (1 − t); deferred tax liabilities rise (or cash falls) by reserve × t.

cards.title: Conversion example
cards.body:
LIFO inventory 800; LIFO reserve beginning 150, ending 200; LIFO COGS 3,000; tax rate 30%.

FIFO inventory = 800 + 200 = **1,000**
FIFO COGS = 3,000 − (200 − 150) = **2,950**
FIFO NI higher by 50 × 0.7 = **35**
FIFO equity higher by 200 × 0.7 = **140**; taxes (DTL) up by 200 × 0.3 = 60.

cards.title: LIFO liquidation
cards.body:
If a LIFO firm sells more than it buys, old cheap layers flow into COGS. In rising prices this **cuts COGS and inflates profit** (and taxes), and the LIFO reserve **falls**.

The extra profit is not sustainable. Red flag: falling LIFO reserve plus rising gross margin. Can be deliberate (delaying purchases to boost earnings) or due to strikes/supply shortages.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Ratios after converting LIFO → FIFO (rising prices): current ratio **up** (more inventory), inventory turnover **down**, gross and net margin **up**, D/E **down** (equity higher). For a single year, use **ΔLIFO reserve** for COGS/NI; use the **level** of the reserve for the balance sheet.

cards.title: Measurement and reversals
rows: LIFO/retail: lower of cost or market (LCM); other methods: lower of cost and NRV
Replacement cost, capped at NRV, floored at NRV − normal margin

cards.title: Write-down and reversal
cards.body:
Cost 100; selling price 95, costs to complete 3, selling costs 2 → NRV = 90.
Write-down = **10** (to 90), expensed (usually in COGS).

Next year NRV recovers to 105.
IFRS: reverse up to original cost → +10 (back to 100), credited to P&L.
US GAAP: no reversal; stays at 90.

cards.title: US GAAP LCM
cards.body:
LIFO item: cost 100; replacement cost 82; NRV 90; normal margin 10 → floor 80.
Market = replacement cost 82 (between 80 and 90).
Write-down = 100 − 82 = **18**.

Under LCNRV the write-down would be only 10.

cards.title: Inventory ratios
cards.formula:
Inventory turnover = COGS ÷ avg inventory
DOH = 365 ÷ inventory turnover
cards.note: High turnover may mean efficiency or inventory too low (lost sales); compare with sales growth.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: IAS 2 NRV rules are familiar. New: US GAAP's **no reversal** rule, the LCM band for LIFO firms, and analyst use of disclosures (LIFO reserve, write-downs, raw/WIP/finished goods mix: rising finished goods with falling raw materials can signal falling demand).

questions.stem: Opening inventory is 100 units at $10. The company buys 200 units at $12 and then 100 units at $15, and sells 250 units. Using periodic LIFO, COGS is:
questions.explanation: LIFO sells the latest units first: 100 × 15 + 150 × 12 = **$3,300**. $2,800 is FIFO; $3,062.50 is weighted average (250 × 12.25).

questions.stem: Which inventory method is permitted under US GAAP but not under IFRS?
questions.explanation: LIFO is prohibited under IAS 2 and permitted under US GAAP. The other two are allowed under both.

questions.stem: In a period of rising prices and stable inventory quantities, compared with FIFO, a LIFO firm will report:
options: lower net income and higher operating cash flow
higher net income and higher taxes
higher ending inventory and lower COGS
questions.explanation: LIFO charges the latest (higher) costs to COGS → lower NI → lower taxes → higher CFO. Inventory is lower under LIFO.

questions.stem: Using the same data (400 units available costing $4,900; 250 sold), ending inventory under weighted average cost is:
A LIFO company reports inventory of $800 and COGS of $3,000. Its LIFO reserve rose from $150 to $200. FIFO COGS is:
questions.explanation: FIFO COGS = 3,000 − (200 − 150) = **$2,950**. $2,800 subtracts the ending reserve level; $3,050 adds the change.

questions.stem: Using the same company (LIFO inventory $800, ending LIFO reserve $200, tax rate 30%), FIFO inventory and the increase in equity from converting to FIFO are:
questions.explanation: FIFO inventory = 800 + 200 = **$1,000**. Equity rises by the after-tax reserve: 200 × 0.7 = **$140**. $200 ignores taxes; $950 adds the beginning reserve ($150) instead of the ending reserve.

questions.stem: A LIFO firm's LIFO reserve falls from $500 to $380 during a period of rising prices. Its LIFO COGS was $4,000. FIFO COGS is:
questions.explanation: FIFO COGS = LIFO COGS − ΔLR = 4,000 − (380 − 500) = **$4,120**. The fall in the reserve signals a LIFO liquidation: old cheap layers lowered LIFO COGS below FIFO this year.

questions.stem: A LIFO liquidation during a period of rising prices will most likely:
questions.explanation: Older, cheaper costs flow into COGS, lowering COGS and raising profit temporarily. The reserve declines.

questions.stem: Inventory cost is $100; estimated selling price $95, costs to complete $3 and selling costs $2. Under IFRS, the write-down is:
questions.explanation: NRV = 95 − 3 − 2 = 90; write-down = 100 − 90 = **$10**. $5 compares cost with selling price only.

questions.stem: Following a previous inventory write-down, the item's NRV recovers above original cost. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Both IFRS and US GAAP allow reversal up to original cost
Neither IFRS nor US GAAP allows reversal
IFRS allows reversal up to original cost; US GAAP prohibits reversal
questions.explanation: IFRS permits reversal limited to the amount of the original write-down; US GAAP prohibits reversing inventory write-downs.

questions.stem: COGS is $3,650 and average inventory is $500. Days of inventory on hand are closest to:
questions.explanation: Turnover = 3,650 ÷ 500 = 7.3; DOH = 365 ÷ 7.3 = **50 days**. 7.3 is the turnover ratio itself.

questions.stem: A US GAAP LIFO firm has an item with cost $100, replacement cost $82, NRV $90 and normal profit margin $10. The inventory write-down is:
questions.explanation: Market = replacement cost bounded by ceiling NRV (90) and floor NRV − margin (80). 82 is within the band, so market = 82 and write-down = **$18**. $10 uses NRV (IFRS/LCNRV); $20 uses the floor.

questions.stem: A LIFO company reports current assets of $1,500 (including inventory of $600) and current liabilities of $1,000. Its LIFO reserve is $300 and the tax rate is 25%. Its current ratio on a FIFO basis (ignoring tax effects on current items) is closest to:
questions.explanation: FIFO current assets = 1,500 + 300 = 1,800; current ratio = 1,800 ÷ 1,000 = **1.80**. 1.50 is the LIFO ratio; 1.73 adds only the after-tax reserve (225).

questions.stem: A LIFO company has total debt of $2,000 and equity of $3,000. Its LIFO reserve is $400 and the tax rate is 25%. Its debt-to-equity ratio adjusted to FIFO is closest to:
questions.explanation: FIFO equity = 3,000 + 400 × 0.75 = 3,300; D/E = 2,000 ÷ 3,300 = **0.61**. 0.67 is the unadjusted LIFO ratio; 0.59 adds the pre-tax reserve to equity.

questions.stem: In a period of rising prices, which method results in the highest inventory turnover ratio?
questions.explanation: LIFO has the highest COGS and the lowest inventory, so COGS ÷ inventory is highest.

questions.stem: An analyst notes that a LIFO company's gross margin increased sharply while its LIFO reserve declined. The most likely explanation is:
questions.explanation: A falling LIFO reserve with a margin spike indicates old low-cost layers were charged to COGS, i.e. a LIFO liquidation. Rising quantities would add new layers, not release old ones.

questions.stem: In a period of falling prices (deflation), compared with FIFO, LIFO will most likely result in:
questions.explanation: In deflation the latest costs are the lowest, so LIFO COGS is lower and ending inventory (older, higher costs) is **higher**. Lower COGS means higher profit and higher taxes.

questions.stem: A company using FIFO under IFRS writes inventory down by $50 in year 1. In year 2, NRV rises by $70. The reversal recognised in year 2 is:
questions.explanation: IFRS allows reversal limited to the original write-down: **$50**. $70 would carry inventory above cost; $0 applies the US GAAP rule.

flashcards.back: Inv_FIFO = Inv_LIFO + LIFO reserve.
COGS_FIFO = COGS_LIFO − ΔLIFO reserve.
NI_FIFO = NI_LIFO + ΔLIFO reserve × (1 − t).
Equity rises by LIFO reserve × (1 − t); deferred tax (or cash) adjusts by reserve × t.
Higher COGS, lower NI, lower taxes, higher CFO, lower inventory, higher turnover, lower current ratio.

flashcards.front: Inventory write-down reversal: IFRS vs US GAAP
flashcards.back: IFRS: allowed up to original cost. US GAAP: prohibited.
Units sold > units bought; old cheap layers hit COGS; profit temporarily up; LIFO reserve falls.
Replacement cost, but not above NRV (ceiling) or below NRV − normal margin (floor). Used for LIFO and retail methods.

modules.title: Analysis of Long-Term Assets
modules.summary: Capitalising vs expensing, intangible assets (including development costs), depreciation and asset-age ratios, impairment under IFRS vs US GAAP, the revaluation model and derecognition.

acca.note: IAS 16, IAS 38 and IAS 36 are FA/FR/SBR core. New for CFA: US GAAP's two-step recoverability test and no-reversal rule, US GAAP expensing of R&D, no revaluation under US GAAP, and analyst ratios for asset age and the financial-statement effects of capitalising.

cards.title: Intangibles and R&D
rows: Capitalise once criteria met (feasibility, intent, ability, future benefit)

cards.title: Capitalised interest
cards.body:
Interest on borrowing to **construct** a qualifying asset is capitalised into its cost (both IFRS and US GAAP). It then hits profit through depreciation.

Analyst adjustments: add capitalised interest back to interest expense for coverage ratios, and move it from CFI to CFO for comparability.

EBIT 600, interest expense 100, capitalised interest 50:
Reported coverage = 600 ÷ 100 = 6.0×; adjusted = 600 ÷ 150 = **4.0×**.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: You know IAS 38's development criteria. The CFA twist: a US GAAP firm **expenses** the same development spend, so an IFRS firm will show higher assets, higher early profit and higher CFO. To compare, analysts may expense IFRS capitalised development or capitalise US R&D.

cards.title: Depreciation methods
cards.formula:
Straight-line = (cost − salvage) ÷ life
DDB = (2 ÷ life) × opening book value
Units of production = (cost − salvage) ÷ total units × units used
where: double-declining balance; ignores salvage until the floor
cards.note: Amortisation of finite-life intangibles works the same way; indefinite-life intangibles are not amortised.

cards.title: SL vs DDB
cards.body:
Cost 50,000; salvage 5,000; life 5 years.

SL = 45,000 ÷ 5 = **9,000** per year.
DDB rate 40%: Y1 = 20,000; Y2 = 12,000; Y3 = 7,200; Y4 = 4,320; Y5 = 1,480 (stops at salvage 5,000).

Accelerated methods → lower early profit, lower early ROA.

cards.title: Asset-age ratios
cards.formula:
Average age = accumulated depreciation ÷ depreciation expense
Total useful life = gross PP&E ÷ depreciation expense
Remaining life = net PP&E ÷ depreciation expense

cards.title: Asset-age example
cards.body:
Gross PP&E 1,200; accumulated depreciation 480; depreciation expense 120.

Average age = 480 ÷ 120 = **4 years**
Total life = 1,200 ÷ 120 = **10 years**
Remaining life = 720 ÷ 120 = **6 years**

An old asset base may signal upcoming heavy capex.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: IAS 16 component depreciation is required under IFRS; US GAAP allows it but it is rare. The new CFA material is the **ratio** side: estimating asset age and spotting earnings management via changes in useful life or salvage value.

cards.title: Impairment of PP&E and finite-life intangibles
rows: One step: carrying amount > recoverable amount
Step 1 recoverability: carrying amount > undiscounted future CF
Carrying − recoverable amount (higher of FV less costs to sell and value in use)
Allowed (not goodwill), up to what carrying amount would have been
Prohibited for assets held and used

cards.title: Same asset, two answers
cards.body:
Carrying amount 1,000; FV less costs to sell 760; value in use 820; undiscounted future cash flows 1,050; fair value 780.

IFRS: recoverable = max(760, 820) = 820 → loss **180**.
US GAAP: undiscounted CF 1,050 > 1,000 → passes recoverability → **no impairment**.

If undiscounted CF were 900: impaired; loss = 1,000 − 780 = **220**.

cards.title: Revaluation model
rows: To OCI (revaluation surplus), unless reversing a prior P&L loss
P&L, unless reversing a prior surplus (then OCI)
Cost or fair value model (FV changes in P&L)

cards.title: Derecognition and held for sale
cards.body:
Sale: gain/loss = proceeds − carrying amount (in P&L; full proceeds in CFI). Cost 80, accumulated depreciation 50, sold for 35 → gain **5**.

Abandoned assets: written off; loss = carrying amount.

Held for sale: stop depreciating; measure at lower of carrying amount and FV less costs to sell (both IFRS and US GAAP); reversals allowed up to earlier write-downs.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Impairment has **no cash effect** at the time (CFO unaffected) but lowers assets and equity and raises future ROA (smaller asset base, less depreciation). Big impairments can be a sign of earlier overstatement or "big bath" accounting.

questions.stem: Compared with expensing, a company that capitalises an expenditure will most likely report in the year of the expenditure:
questions.explanation: Capitalised spending is an investing outflow (CFI), so CFO is **higher**. Assets are higher, not lower.

questions.stem: Under US GAAP, costs incurred in the development phase of an internal project (other than software) are generally:
options: capitalised once technical feasibility is established
questions.explanation: US GAAP generally expenses R&D. IFRS capitalises development costs once criteria are met; US GAAP capitalisation applies only to specific software costs.

questions.stem: EBIT is $600, interest expense is $100 and interest capitalised during the year is $50. Interest coverage adjusted for capitalised interest is:
questions.explanation: Adjusted coverage = 600 ÷ (100 + 50) = **4.0×**. 6.0× is the reported ratio; 12.0× uses capitalised interest alone.

questions.stem: An IFRS company capitalises development costs that a US GAAP peer expenses. All else equal, the IFRS company will most likely report a:
questions.explanation: Capitalising raises assets and equity, lowering D/E. It raises CFO and smooths earnings.

questions.stem: An asset costs $50,000, has a salvage value of $5,000 and a five-year life. Depreciation in year 2 under double-declining balance is:
Gross PP&E is $1,200, accumulated depreciation $480 and annual depreciation $120. The estimated remaining useful life is:
questions.explanation: Remaining life = net PP&E ÷ depreciation = (1,200 − 480) ÷ 120 = **6 years**. 4 is average age; 10 is total life.

questions.stem: A machine costs $100,000 with salvage of $10,000 and is expected to produce 300,000 units. In year 1 it produces 45,000 units. Units-of-production depreciation is:
Relative to straight-line, an accelerated depreciation method in the early years of an asset's life results in:
questions.explanation: Accelerated methods charge more depreciation early, reducing NI and net book value.

questions.stem: An asset has a carrying amount of $1,000, fair value less costs to sell of $760, value in use of $820 and undiscounted future cash flows of $1,050. The impairment loss under IFRS is:
questions.explanation: Recoverable amount = higher of 760 and 820 = 820; loss = 1,000 − 820 = **$180**. $240 uses the lower measure; $0 applies the US GAAP recoverability test.

questions.stem: Using the same asset (carrying $1,000, fair value $780, undiscounted cash flows $1,050), the impairment loss under US GAAP is:
questions.explanation: Step 1: undiscounted CF of 1,050 exceed carrying amount of 1,000, so the asset is recoverable and **no impairment** is recognised. $220 would apply only if it failed step 1.

questions.stem: Under IFRS, a company revalues land upward by $100 (no previous impairment). The increase is reported in:
questions.explanation: Upward revaluations go to OCI/revaluation surplus unless they reverse a decrease previously charged to P&L.

questions.stem: Equipment with a cost of $80 and accumulated depreciation of $50 is sold for $35. The company reports:
options: a $5 gain and a $35 investing inflow
a $45 loss and a $35 investing inflow
a $5 gain and a $5 operating inflow
questions.explanation: Carrying amount = 30; gain = 35 − 30 = **$5** in P&L. The full $35 proceeds are a CFI inflow; the gain is removed from CFO.

questions.stem: An IFRS company revalued a building from $500 to $600, recording $100 in revaluation surplus. Two years later (ignore depreciation) the building's fair value falls to $450. The amounts recognised are:
options: $100 reduction in OCI and $50 loss in profit or loss
questions.explanation: The decrease first reverses the existing surplus of $100 through OCI; the remaining $50 is a loss in **P&L**. A full P&L loss ignores the surplus; a full OCI charge exceeds the surplus available.

questions.stem: Which statement about impairment reversals is most accurate?
options: Both IFRS and US GAAP permit reversals of PP&E impairments
IFRS permits reversals of PP&E impairments; US GAAP prohibits them for assets held and used
Neither permits reversal of goodwill impairment except under IFRS
questions.explanation: IFRS allows reversal (except goodwill) up to the carrying amount that would have existed without the impairment. US GAAP prohibits reversal for held-and-used assets. Goodwill impairments are never reversed under either.

questions.stem: Company A (IFRS) capitalises $40 million of development costs; Company B (US GAAP) spends the same and expenses it. In the year of spending, compared with B, A will report:
options: higher net income and higher CFO
higher net income and the same CFO
questions.explanation: Capitalising keeps the cost off the income statement (higher NI) and classifies the outflow in CFI rather than CFO (higher CFO, lower CFI).

questions.stem: A US GAAP company's asset fails the recoverability test. The impairment loss is measured as the carrying amount minus:
questions.explanation: Under US GAAP, once impaired, loss = carrying amount − **fair value** (or discounted CF if FV unavailable). Undiscounted cash flows are used only for the recoverability step; value in use is an IFRS concept.

questions.stem: Compared with the cost model, an IFRS company using the fair value model for investment property reports:
options: fair value changes in OCI and depreciation
fair value changes in profit or loss and no depreciation
questions.explanation: Under the IAS 40 fair value model, gains and losses go to **P&L** and the property is not depreciated. This differs from the IAS 16 revaluation model, where gains go to OCI. US GAAP has no fair value model for investment property.

questions.stem: An analyst notices that a company extended the useful lives of its equipment from 8 to 12 years while peers kept 8 years. The most likely effect is:
options: higher reported earnings with no change in cash flow
questions.explanation: Longer lives cut depreciation, raising NI. There is no cash effect (ignoring taxes in book-only changes). This is a classic earnings-management warning sign.

flashcards.back: Impaired if carrying amount > recoverable amount = max(FV − costs to sell, value in use). Loss = carrying − recoverable. Reversal allowed (not goodwill).

flashcards.front: US GAAP impairment test (held and used)
flashcards.back: Step 1: carrying > undiscounted future CF? Step 2: loss = carrying − fair value. No reversal.

flashcards.front: Development costs: IFRS vs US GAAP
flashcards.back: IFRS: capitalise once criteria met. US GAAP: expense (except certain software).
IFRS only (PP&E; intangibles with active market). Up → OCI unless reversing prior P&L loss; down → P&L unless reversing prior surplus.
Accumulated depreciation ÷ depreciation expense.
Net PP&E ÷ depreciation expense.
Capitalise → outflow in CFI → higher CFO, lower CFI. Total cash flow unchanged.
No depreciation; lower of carrying amount and FV less costs to sell.

modules.title: Topics in Long-Term Liabilities and Equity
modules.summary: Lease accounting for lessees (IFRS 16 single model vs ASC 842 finance and operating leases) and lessors, defined benefit vs defined contribution pensions, and share-based compensation.

acca.note: IFRS 16 lessee accounting, IAS 19 and IFRS 2 are FR/SBR topics. New for CFA: ASC 842 operating leases (single straight-line lease cost), US GAAP lessor categories, cash-flow classification of lease payments, and analyst effects on EBITDA, coverage and leverage.

cards.title: Lessee basics
cards.body:
At inception the lessee records a **right-of-use (ROU) asset** and a **lease liability** = PV of lease payments (at the implicit rate or incremental borrowing rate).

Exemptions: short-term leases (≤ 12 months) under both; low-value assets under IFRS only.

Under IFRS 16 every other lease is treated like a finance lease. US GAAP (ASC 842) keeps **two** lessee models.

cards.title: Income statement and cash flow
rows: Single straight-line lease cost (in operating expenses)

cards.title: Five-year lease
cards.body:
Payments 10,000 a year in arrears, 5 years, rate 6%.
Liability = ROU = **42,123.64**.

IFRS/finance, year 1: interest 2,527.42 + depreciation 8,424.73 = **10,952.15**. Liability end = 42,123.64 + 2,527.42 − 10,000 = 34,651.06.

ASC 842 operating, year 1: lease cost **10,000** (straight-line); ROU is the plug so it equals the liability (34,651.06).

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: You know IFRS 16 cold. What is new is the **US GAAP operating lease**: same balance sheet, but one straight-line cost in operating expenses and the **whole payment in CFO**. So vs IFRS 16 it shows lower EBITDA, lower EBIT, lower CFO, and flat (not front-loaded) expense.

cards.title: Lessor accounting
rows: Derecognise asset; record net investment (receivable); interest income; selling profit at inception if any
Same idea; direct financing defers selling profit
Keep and depreciate asset; lease income straight-line

cards.title: DC vs DB pensions
rows: Service cost + net interest (+ other items)

cards.title: DB funded status
cards.body:
Net pension liability = PV of defined benefit obligation − fair value of plan assets.

DBO 1,000; plan assets 900 → **net liability 100** (underfunded).

IFRS: service cost and net interest (discount rate × net liability) in P&L; remeasurements (actuarial gains/losses, return on assets above interest) in **OCI**, never recycled. US GAAP P&L also includes expected return and amortised OCI items.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Analysts treat an underfunded DB plan as **debt-like**: add the net pension liability to debt when computing leverage. Watch assumptions: a higher discount rate lowers the obligation and makes the plan look healthier.

cards.title: Why it matters
cards.body: Stock grants and options align managers with shareholders, but they cost existing owners via **dilution**. Both IFRS 2 and ASC 718 require an expense measured at **grant-date fair value**, spread over the **vesting (service) period**.

cards.title: Option expense
cards.body:
100,000 options granted, fair value $4 each at grant, vest over 4 years.

Total cost = 400,000 → expense **100,000** per year.

Later share-price changes do not change the expense for equity-settled options. A higher volatility or longer expected term assumption raises fair value and the expense.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: Same IFRS 2 principles. CFA stresses disclosure analysis: option-pricing assumptions (volatility, expected life, risk-free rate, dividend yield) are management choices, and lowering volatility shrinks the expense. Options are also added to diluted EPS via the treasury stock method.

questions.stem: A lessee signs a 5-year lease with annual payments of $10,000 in arrears. The discount rate is 6%. The lease liability at inception is closest to:
questions.explanation: PV of a 5-year $10,000 annuity at 6% = **$42,124**. $50,000 ignores discounting; $44,651 treats payments as an annuity due.

questions.stem: For the lease above (liability $42,124, straight-line depreciation over 5 years), total year 1 expense under IFRS 16 is closest to:
questions.explanation: Interest = 6% × 42,124 = 2,527; depreciation = 42,124 ÷ 5 = 8,425; total = **$10,952**. $10,000 is the US GAAP operating lease cost; $8,425 is depreciation alone.

questions.stem: Under ASC 842, a lessee's payments on an operating lease are classified in the cash flow statement as:
options: interest in operating, principal in financing
questions.explanation: US GAAP operating lease payments are all **CFO**. The split (interest CFO, principal CFF) applies to US GAAP finance leases; IFRS lets interest be CFO or CFF.

questions.stem: Compared with an identical US GAAP lessee classifying the lease as operating, an IFRS 16 lessee will most likely report:
questions.explanation: IFRS 16 expense is depreciation + interest, neither of which is in EBITDA, and the principal portion is in CFF. Both raise EBITDA and CFO vs the US operating model. Liabilities are the same.

questions.stem: In a defined contribution pension plan, investment risk is borne by:
questions.explanation: In a DC plan the employer only promises contributions; the eventual benefit depends on investment returns, so the **employee** bears the risk.

questions.stem: A DB plan has an obligation of $1,000 and plan assets with fair value of $900. The balance sheet shows:
options: a liability of $1,000 and an asset of $900
questions.explanation: Funded status = 900 − 1,000 = −100 → **net liability of $100**. Obligations and assets are netted, not shown gross.

questions.stem: Under IFRS, actuarial gains and losses on a defined benefit plan are recognised in:
options: OCI and later amortised to profit or loss
questions.explanation: IFRS remeasurements go to OCI and are never recycled. US GAAP puts actuarial gains/losses in OCI and amortises them to P&L (corridor approach).

questions.stem: Under ASC 842, a lessor that transfers control of the asset and recognises selling profit at inception has a:
questions.explanation: A sales-type lease recognises selling profit at commencement. A direct financing lease defers it; an operating lease keeps the asset on the lessor's books.

questions.stem: A company grants 100,000 options with a grant-date fair value of $4 each, vesting over 4 years. Annual compensation expense is:
questions.explanation: Total = 100,000 × $4 = 400,000, spread over 4 years = **$100,000** per year.

questions.stem: Which change in assumptions would most likely reduce the reported expense for newly granted stock options?
questions.explanation: Lower volatility lowers option value and thus the expense. Higher volatility or longer term increase it.

questions.stem: Compensation expense for equity-settled stock options is based on fair value measured at:
questions.explanation: Grant-date fair value, recognised over the vesting period. Cash-settled awards (SARs) are remeasured each reporting date.

questions.stem: A US GAAP lessee classifies a lease as operating. Compared with classifying the same lease as a finance lease, in year 1 the operating classification results in:
options: the same total liabilities but higher interest expense
questions.explanation: Operating: whole payment in CFO and a single lease cost in operating expenses (reducing EBIT by more than depreciation alone). Finance: principal in CFF and interest below EBIT. So the operating model gives **lower CFO and lower EBIT**. There is no interest expense under the operating model.

questions.stem: For the 5-year, $10,000-per-year, 6% lease (initial liability $42,124), the lease liability at the end of year 1 is closest to:
questions.explanation: Liability = 42,124 + 6% × 42,124 − 10,000 = **$34,651**. $32,124 ignores interest; $33,699 is the IFRS ROU asset after one year of straight-line depreciation.

questions.stem: Under IFRS 16, which lease may the lessee keep off the balance sheet?
options: A lease of a low-value laptop
questions.explanation: IFRS exempts short-term (≤ 12 months) and low-value leases. IFRS 16 has no operating lease category for lessees. A 3-year lease is not short-term.

questions.stem: An analyst adjusting leverage for an underfunded defined benefit plan would most likely:
options: add the net pension liability to debt
ignore it because it is not interest-bearing
questions.explanation: An underfunded DB plan is a debt-like obligation; analysts often add the net liability (often after tax) to debt.

questions.stem: Stock appreciation rights settled in cash are accounted for as:
options: equity, measured once at grant date
a liability remeasured at fair value each period
questions.explanation: Cash-settled awards create a liability that is remeasured at each reporting date until settlement, with changes in expense.

questions.stem: Under IFRS 16, a lessee's total lease-related expense over the life of a lease, compared with total lease payments, is:
questions.explanation: Over the full term total expense (depreciation + interest) equals total payments (ignoring initial direct costs); IFRS just front-loads it.

flashcards.back: Single model: ROU asset + lease liability; depreciation + interest. Exemptions: short-term and low-value.
ROU asset + liability on BS; single straight-line lease cost in operating expenses; entire payment in CFO.

flashcards.front: Lease payment cash flows: finance lease
flashcards.back: Interest: CFO (US GAAP), CFO or CFF (IFRS). Principal: CFF.
IFRS: finance or operating. US GAAP: sales-type, direct financing, operating.
PV of defined benefit obligation − FV of plan assets.

flashcards.front: IFRS DB pension: P&L vs OCI
flashcards.back: P&L: service cost + net interest. OCI: remeasurements (not recycled).
Grant-date fair value expensed over the vesting period; cash-settled awards remeasured as liabilities.

modules.title: Analysis of Income Taxes
modules.summary: Accounting vs taxable profit, temporary and permanent differences, deferred tax assets and liabilities, valuation allowances, and effective, statutory and cash tax rates.

acca.note: IAS 12 (carrying amount vs tax base) is FR/SBR material. New for CFA: US GAAP valuation allowance terminology, cash tax rate and tax-rate reconciliation analysis, and analyst treatment of DTLs as debt or equity.

cards.title: Core relationships
cards.formula:
Income tax expense = taxes payable + ΔDTL − ΔDTA
DTL/DTA = (carrying amount − tax base) × tax rate
where: tax on taxable income (from the tax return)
value of an item for tax purposes
cards.note: Asset: carrying > tax base → DTL. Liability: carrying > tax base → DTA.

cards.title: Accelerated tax depreciation
cards.body:
