Asset cost 90,000; book SL 3 years (30,000/yr); tax depreciation in year 1 = 45,000; tax rate 30%.

End of year 1: carrying amount 60,000; tax base 45,000.
DTL = 15,000 × 30% = **4,500**.

The DTL reverses as book depreciation catches up.

cards.title: Common sources
rows: Warranty or restructuring provision (deductible when paid)
Revenue received in advance, taxed on receipt

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: IAS 12 logic is identical. CFA vocabulary: **taxes payable** = current tax; **income tax expense** = current + deferred; **taxable income** vs **accounting profit (pretax income)**. Under US GAAP, deferred taxes are always classified as **non-current** (same as IFRS).

lessons.title: Tax rates, permanent differences and valuation allowances

cards.title: Permanent vs temporary
cards.body:
**Temporary** differences reverse (depreciation timing, provisions) → deferred tax.
**Permanent** differences never reverse (non-deductible fines, tax-exempt interest, some meals) → **no deferred tax**; they make the effective tax rate differ from the statutory rate.

Pretax 1,000; non-deductible fines 60; tax-exempt income 20; rate 25% → tax = 1,040 × 25% = 260 → ETR **26%**.

cards.title: Tax rates
cards.formula:
Effective tax rate = income tax expense ÷ pretax income
Cash tax rate = cash taxes paid ÷ pretax income
cards.note: The tax-rate reconciliation in the notes explains statutory vs effective; look for one-offs and unsustainable benefits.

cards.title: Recognising DTAs
rows: Recognise only to the extent **probable** that taxable profit will be available
Recognise in full, then reduce with a **valuation allowance** if more likely than not (>50%) it will not be realised
Changes in recognised DTA hit earnings
Changes in the allowance hit earnings; a falling allowance can boost profit

cards.title: Tax rate changes and analyst treatment
cards.body:
When the rate changes, existing DTLs and DTAs are remeasured at the new rate and the difference goes through tax expense (or OCI if the original item went to OCI).

DTL 300 at 30%; rate falls to 25% → DTL = 300 ÷ 0.30 × 0.25 = **250**; tax expense falls by 50.

Analysts treat a DTL **not expected to reverse** (growing capex) as equity; one expected to reverse as a liability.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: A lower tax rate **reduces** DTLs (good for equity) but **reduces** DTAs (bad: write-down increases tax expense). Don't assume a rate cut always raises net income.

questions.stem: Taxes payable are $300, the DTL increased by $20 and the DTA increased by $5. Income tax expense is:
questions.explanation: Tax expense = 300 + 20 − 5 = **$315**. $325 adds the DTA increase; $285 subtracts the DTL increase.

questions.stem: An asset has a carrying amount of $600 and a tax base of $450. The tax rate is 25%. The company reports a:
questions.explanation: Asset carrying > tax base → future taxable amounts → DTL = 150 × 25% = **$37.50**. $150 is the temporary difference before applying the rate.

questions.stem: A company accrues a warranty provision of $200 that is deductible for tax only when paid. With a 25% tax rate this creates:
options: no deferred tax because it is a permanent difference
questions.explanation: The liability's carrying amount (200) exceeds its tax base (0); future deductions create a **DTA** of 200 × 25% = $50. It reverses when paid, so it is temporary.

questions.stem: An asset costs $90,000. Book depreciation is straight-line over 3 years; tax depreciation is $45,000 in year 1. With a 30% tax rate, the DTL at the end of year 1 is:
questions.explanation: Carrying 60,000 − tax base 45,000 = 15,000 × 30% = **$4,500**. $9,000 applies the rate to book depreciation; $13,500 applies it to tax depreciation.

questions.stem: Pretax income is $1,000, including $20 of tax-exempt interest, and $60 of fines that are not tax-deductible were deducted. The statutory rate is 25%. The effective tax rate is:
questions.explanation: Taxable income = 1,000 − 20 + 60 = 1,040; tax = 260; ETR = 260 ÷ 1,000 = **26%**. 25% ignores the permanent differences; 24% reverses their direction.

questions.stem: A company has a DTL of $300 measured at a 30% tax rate. The tax rate is cut to 25%. The DTL becomes:
options: $360 and income tax expense increases by $60
$250 and income tax expense decreases by $50
$250 and income tax expense increases by $50
questions.explanation: DTL = 300 ÷ 0.30 × 0.25 = **$250**; the $50 reduction lowers tax expense.

questions.stem: Under US GAAP, a valuation allowance is recorded when:
options: it is more likely than not that some of a DTA will not be realised
a DTL is not expected to reverse
the effective tax rate exceeds the statutory rate
questions.explanation: A valuation allowance reduces a DTA when realisation is not more likely than not. IFRS instead recognises DTAs only to the extent probable.

questions.stem: Which item most likely creates a permanent difference?
options: A warranty provision deductible when paid
questions.explanation: A non-deductible fine never reverses → permanent difference. The other two are temporary differences.

questions.stem: A company reports pretax income of $1,000. Due to accelerated tax depreciation, taxable income is $900. The tax rate is 25% and there are no other differences. Income tax expense and the change in DTL are:
questions.explanation: Taxes payable = 900 × 25% = 225. Book exceeds tax income by 100 (timing), so DTL rises by 25. Tax expense = 225 + 25 = **$250**. $225 is taxes payable only; accelerated tax depreciation creates a DTL, not a DTA.

questions.stem: A company paid cash taxes of $230 on pretax income of $1,000 and reported income tax expense of $260. Its cash tax rate is:
questions.explanation: Cash tax rate = 230 ÷ 1,000 = **23%**. 26% is the effective tax rate.

questions.stem: A US GAAP company reduces its valuation allowance because it now expects future taxable profits. All else equal, this will:
options: decrease income tax expense and increase net income
questions.explanation: Reducing the allowance increases the net DTA, with the credit going to deferred tax expense, so tax expense falls and NI rises. Analysts check whether the reversal is justified.

questions.stem: A company's DTL relates to equipment and has grown every year because capital spending keeps increasing. An analyst would most likely treat this DTL as:
options: a liability, because it will reverse soon
equity, because it is not expected to reverse
questions.explanation: If the DTL is not expected to reverse in the foreseeable future, analysts treat it as equity (reduce liabilities, increase equity).

questions.stem: A company has a DTA of $120 measured at a 30% tax rate. The rate is cut to 25%. Income tax expense will:
questions.explanation: New DTA = 120 ÷ 0.30 × 0.25 = 100; the $20 reduction in the asset **increases** tax expense.

questions.stem: Under IFRS, deferred tax arising from an upward revaluation of PP&E is recognised in:
questions.explanation: Deferred tax follows the underlying item: the revaluation gain is in OCI, so the related DTL is charged to **OCI**.

flashcards.back: Taxes payable + ΔDTL − ΔDTA.
Asset: carrying > tax base → DTL. Liability: carrying > tax base → DTA.
Never reverses (fines, tax-exempt income). No deferred tax; causes ETR ≠ statutory rate.
ETR = tax expense ÷ pretax income. Cash tax rate = cash taxes paid ÷ pretax income.

flashcards.front: DTA recognition: IFRS vs US GAAP
flashcards.back: IFRS: recognise to extent probable. US GAAP: recognise in full, less valuation allowance if more likely than not unrealised.

flashcards.front: Effect of a tax rate cut
flashcards.back: DTLs and DTAs both fall. DTL fall → lower tax expense; DTA fall → higher tax expense.
Expected to reverse → liability. Not expected to reverse → equity.

modules.title: Financial Reporting Quality
modules.summary: Reporting quality vs earnings quality, the quality spectrum, motivations and conditions for manipulation, discipline mechanisms, non-GAAP measures, accounting choices that manage earnings, cash flow and the balance sheet, and warning signs.

acca.note: AA covered fraud risk and auditor responsibilities; SBR covered ethics in reporting. New for CFA: the quality spectrum, the analyst's checklist of choices used to manage earnings and cash flow, non-GAAP measures and specific red flags.

cards.title: Two kinds of quality
cards.body:
**Financial reporting quality**: are the statements useful, complying with GAAP and faithfully representing economic reality?
**Earnings (results) quality**: are the earnings **sustainable** and adequate (a good return on capital)?

High reporting quality is a precondition: you cannot judge earnings quality if the reporting is poor.

cards.title: Quality spectrum (best to worst)
rows: GAAP-compliant, decision-useful, sustainable and adequate returns
GAAP, decision-useful, but low earnings quality (unsustainable or inadequate)
GAAP, but biased choices (conservative or aggressive)
GAAP, but earnings management via real actions or choices

cards.title: Conservative vs aggressive
cards.body:
**Aggressive** choices raise current earnings or assets (e.g. long useful lives, low bad-debt allowance). **Conservative** choices lower them now (e.g. big provisions).

Both are biased. "Cookie jar" reserves made conservatively today can be released later to smooth or inflate earnings. Conservatism is not automatically good quality.

cards.title: Why and when it happens
cards.body:
**Motivations**: meet analyst forecasts, protect bonus or share price, avoid covenant breaches, career concerns.

**Conditions** (fraud triangle):
- **Opportunity** (weak controls, weak board, complex standards)
- **Motivation/pressure**
- **Rationalisation** ("we'll fix it next quarter")

**Discipline**: regulators (SEC registration and review), auditors, boards and audit committees, private contracts (lenders), and investors.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: AA framed the fraud triangle for **auditors**. CFA uses it from the **analyst's** side: judge whether conditions exist and then test the numbers. Expect questions asking where a scenario sits on the quality spectrum.

cards.title: Common choices
rows: Bill-and-hold, channel stuffing, gross vs net reporting as principal, front-loading multi-element deals
Long useful lives, high salvage values, capitalising operating costs, low bad-debt/warranty allowances
Stretching payables, selling receivables (factoring), classifying operating outflows as investing

cards.title: Managing CFO
cards.body:
CFO can be dressed up too:
- **Delay paying suppliers** (stretch payables): raises CFO once, not sustainable
- **Sell or securitise receivables**: cash arrives early in CFO
- **Capitalise** costs: outflow moves to CFI
- IFRS choices: put interest paid in CFF or interest/dividends received in CFO

Check whether CFO growth is backed by NI growth and stable working capital days.

cards.title: Warning signs
rows: NI growing much faster than CFO (high accruals)
Receivables growth > revenue growth; rising DSO

cards.title: Non-GAAP measures
cards.body:
Adjusted EBITDA, "core" earnings, etc. are unaudited and company-defined. Regulators (SEC Reg G, ESMA guidelines) require: the most comparable GAAP measure shown **with equal or greater prominence**, a **reconciliation**, and an explanation of usefulness.

Red flag: adjustments that always increase earnings, or that change definition year to year.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: "Which is a warning sign?" questions usually point to a **mismatch**: an accrual line (receivables, inventory, NI) moving faster than its economic driver (revenue, sales, CFO). A ratio moving the right way can still be a red flag if it diverges from peers.

questions.stem: A company's statements comply with GAAP and are decision-useful, but its earnings depend on a one-off asset sale and are not expected to recur. This is best described as:
options: high financial reporting quality but low earnings quality
questions.explanation: Reporting is GAAP-compliant and useful (high reporting quality), but earnings are not sustainable (low earnings quality). Nothing suggests fraud.

questions.stem: In the fraud triangle, weak internal controls and an ineffective board most directly represent:
questions.explanation: Weak controls and governance give the **opportunity** to manipulate. Motivation is pressure; rationalisation is the internal justification.

questions.stem: A company records a very large restructuring provision in a bad year and releases part of it into income in later years. This is most likely an example of:
options: creating a "cookie jar" reserve to manage earnings
questions.explanation: Over-providing in a bad year and releasing later smooths earnings. Biased conservatism is still low quality; it is not a policy change.

questions.stem: Which ranks lowest on the financial reporting quality spectrum?
questions.explanation: Fictitious transactions (fraud) are the bottom of the spectrum, below non-compliant reporting, which is below biased GAAP choices.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely a warning sign of aggressive revenue recognition?
options: DSO rising steadily while revenue growth accelerates
Inventory turnover rising in line with peers
CFO growing faster than net income
questions.explanation: Rising DSO with accelerating revenue suggests revenue is being booked before cash is collectible (e.g. channel stuffing). CFO > NI growth is a sign of good quality; normal inventory turnover is not a concern.

questions.stem: A company boosts reported CFO by delaying payments to suppliers at year-end. This is best described as:
options: a sustainable improvement in cash generation
a temporary, unsustainable cash-flow management tactic
questions.explanation: Stretching payables raises CFO once but cannot continue indefinitely and will reverse. It is not a policy change.

questions.stem: When a company reports a non-GAAP measure in a filing, regulators generally require it to:
options: replace the GAAP measure in the headline
present the most comparable GAAP measure and a reconciliation
questions.explanation: Rules such as SEC Regulation G require the comparable GAAP measure (with equal or greater prominence) and a reconciliation. Non-GAAP measures are not separately audited and cannot replace GAAP measures.

questions.stem: A company classifies certain recurring software maintenance costs as capital expenditure. Relative to expensing, this most likely:
options: has no effect on cash flow classification
questions.explanation: Capitalising moves the outflow to CFI (higher CFO) and delays the expense (higher current NI): both flatter the company.

questions.stem: Over three years a company's net income grew 15% per year while CFO declined, receivables rose from 45 to 70 days of sales, and the company introduced an "adjusted EBITDA" measure that excludes stock compensation and restructuring costs every year. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: Earnings quality appears high because net income is growing
Only the non-GAAP measure is a concern
Several warning signs suggest low earnings quality
questions.explanation: NI rising while CFO falls, rising DSO, and recurring exclusions in a non-GAAP measure are all red flags pointing to low earnings quality.

questions.stem: Which accounting choice is most likely considered aggressive?
options: Shortening estimated useful lives of equipment
Raising estimated salvage values of equipment
Increasing the allowance for doubtful accounts
questions.explanation: Higher salvage values reduce depreciation and raise current earnings: aggressive. The other two reduce current earnings (conservative).

questions.stem: A distributor ships unusually large volumes to customers in the last week of the year, with generous return rights. This practice is known as:
questions.explanation: Pushing excess inventory into the channel to book revenue early is **channel stuffing**, often seen as a Q4 revenue spike and rising receivables. Big bath accounting means taking excessive charges in a bad year.

questions.stem: Which mechanism is least likely to discipline financial reporting quality?
options: Debt covenants that rely on reported numbers
Management bonuses tied to reported earnings
questions.explanation: Earnings-based bonuses create **motivation** to manipulate. Audits and lenders monitoring covenants act as discipline (although covenants can also create pressure, lenders scrutinise the numbers).

questions.stem: An analyst finds that a company's inventory has grown 30% while sales grew 5%. The most likely concern is:
options: obsolete or slow-moving inventory that may need a write-down
questions.explanation: Inventory growing much faster than sales suggests weak demand or obsolescence and possible future write-downs (and possibly overproduction to absorb fixed costs).

flashcards.back: Reporting quality: decision-useful, faithful, GAAP-compliant information. Earnings quality: sustainable and adequate earnings. Reporting quality must be high to judge earnings quality.
Opportunity, motivation (pressure), rationalisation.
Fictitious transactions (fraud), below departures from GAAP.
Stretch payables, sell/securitise receivables, capitalise operating costs, IFRS classification choices for interest/dividends.
Show comparable GAAP measure with equal or greater prominence; reconcile; explain usefulness.
NI growing faster than CFO for several periods; receivables or inventory growing faster than revenue.

modules.title: Financial Analysis Techniques
modules.summary: Tools for analysis (ratios, common-size, trend and cross-sectional analysis), activity, liquidity, solvency, profitability and valuation ratios, DuPont decomposition and industry-specific ratios.

acca.note: FR interpretation and FM working-capital ratios (cash conversion cycle) overlap heavily. New for CFA: exact CFA ratio definitions (averages, purchases for DPO), defensive interval, fixed-charge coverage, the 3- and 5-step DuPont, and interpreting ratio changes.

cards.title: Activity ratios
cards.formula:
Receivables turnover = revenue ÷ avg AR; DSO = 365 ÷ turnover
Inventory turnover = COGS ÷ avg inventory; DOH = 365 ÷ turnover
Payables turnover = purchases ÷ avg AP; DPO = 365 ÷ turnover
Total asset turnover = revenue ÷ avg TA
cards.note: Fixed asset turnover = revenue ÷ avg net fixed assets; working capital turnover = revenue ÷ avg working capital.

cards.title: Cash conversion cycle
cards.body:
Revenue 7,300; avg AR 900 → turnover 8.11, **DSO 45**.
COGS 5,475; avg inventory 750 → turnover 7.3, **DOH 50**.
Purchases 5,840; avg AP 640 → turnover 9.125, **DPO 40**.

CCC = DSO + DOH − DPO = 45 + 50 − 40 = **55 days**.

cards.title: Extra liquidity measures
cards.formula:
Defensive interval = (cash + ST securities + receivables) ÷ daily cash expenditures
CCC = DSO + DOH − DPO
cards.note: Defensive interval: how many days the firm can pay expenses from liquid assets with no new revenue.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: FM's "receivables days" and "inventory days" are CFA's **DSO** and **DOH**. Differences: CFA uses **average** balances and **purchases** (not COGS) for payables turnover. A shorter CCC is generally better, but a very high payables period may signal liquidity strain.

cards.title: Coverage ratios
cards.formula:
Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ interest expense
Fixed charge coverage = (EBIT + lease payments) ÷ (interest + lease payments)
where: operating lease payments added back to both
cards.note: EBIT 600, interest 120, lease payments 80: coverage = 5.0×; fixed charge coverage = 680 ÷ 200 = 3.4×.

cards.title: Profitability ratios
rows: NI ÷ avg TA (or [NI + interest × (1 − t)] ÷ avg TA)

cards.title: Valuation and growth
rows: Price ÷ per-share EPS, cash flow, sales, book value

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Know what each ratio **mixes**: income-statement ÷ balance-sheet ratios (turnover, ROA, ROE) use **average** balance-sheet figures. Gross margin falling while operating margin is stable means overheads were cut while pricing or input costs worsened.

cards.title: 3-step DuPont
cards.formula: ROE = (NI ÷ revenue) × (revenue ÷ avg TA) × (avg TA ÷ avg equity)

cards.title: 5-step DuPont
cards.formula: ROE = (NI ÷ EBT) × (EBT ÷ EBIT) × (EBIT ÷ revenue) × (revenue ÷ avg TA) × (avg TA ÷ avg equity)

cards.title: Reading DuPont
cards.body:
Ask **which lever** moved ROE:
- Better margin or turnover → operating improvement (good quality)
- Higher leverage → more financial risk

More debt raises leverage but lowers the interest burden (more interest), so net effect depends on whether the return on assets beats the after-tax cost of debt. A lower tax burden ratio means a **higher** tax rate.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: "Tax burden" and "interest burden" are named backwards from intuition: a ratio of **1.0 means no tax / no interest**. If interest burden falls from 0.90 to 0.80, interest costs went **up**.

questions.stem: A company has DSO of 45 days, DOH of 50 days and DPO of 40 days. Its cash conversion cycle is:
questions.explanation: CCC = 45 + 50 − 40 = **55 days**. 135 adds DPO; 35 subtracts DOH.

questions.stem: Purchases are $5,840 and average accounts payable are $640. Days of payables outstanding are closest to:
questions.explanation: Payables turnover = 5,840 ÷ 640 = 9.125; DPO = 365 ÷ 9.125 = **40 days**. 9.1 is the turnover.

questions.stem: Cash is $100, ST marketable securities $50, receivables $150, and daily cash expenditures are $10. The defensive interval is:
questions.explanation: (100 + 50 + 150) ÷ 10 = **30 days**. 15 excludes receivables; 25 excludes marketable securities.

questions.stem: A company's receivables turnover fell from 10× to 8× while peers were stable. This most likely indicates:
options: slower collection or looser credit terms
questions.explanation: Lower turnover = higher DSO (36.5 → 45.6 days): slower collection or more generous credit. It does not by itself indicate lower sales.

questions.stem: EBIT is $600, interest expense $120 and lease payments $80. Fixed charge coverage is:
questions.explanation: (600 + 80) ÷ (120 + 80) = **3.4×**. 5.0× is interest coverage; 7.5× is EBIT ÷ lease payments.

questions.stem: ROE is 15% and the dividend payout ratio is 40%. The sustainable growth rate is:
questions.explanation: g = b × ROE = (1 − 0.40) × 15% = **9%**. 6% uses the payout ratio instead of retention.

questions.stem: Which ratio uses EBIT in the numerator and the sum of debt and equity in the denominator?
questions.explanation: Return on total capital = EBIT ÷ (debt + equity). ROE uses NI ÷ equity; operating margin uses EBIT ÷ revenue.

questions.stem: A firm's gross margin fell from 40% to 36% while its operating margin was unchanged. The most likely explanation is:
options: higher operating expenses relative to sales
lower operating expenses relative to sales offsetting weaker gross profit
questions.explanation: Operating margin = gross margin − opex ratio. If gross margin fell 4 points and operating margin is unchanged, opex as a % of sales must have fallen. Interest is below operating income.

questions.stem: A company has a net margin of 5%, asset turnover of 1.6 and financial leverage of 2.5. ROE is:
questions.explanation: ROE = 0.05 × 1.6 × 2.5 = **20%**. 8% omits leverage; 12.5% omits turnover.

questions.stem: Tax burden 0.75, interest burden 0.80, EBIT margin 12%, asset turnover 1.2 and leverage 2.0. ROE is closest to:
questions.explanation: ROE = 0.75 × 0.80 × 0.12 × 1.2 × 2.0 = **17.28%**. 21.6% omits the interest burden; 8.6% omits leverage.

questions.stem: A company's interest burden ratio fell from 0.90 to 0.80. This most likely means:
options: interest expense fell relative to EBIT
interest expense rose relative to EBIT
questions.explanation: Interest burden = EBT ÷ EBIT. A lower ratio means a bigger gap between EBIT and EBT, i.e. more interest relative to EBIT.

questions.stem: ROE rose from 12% to 15%. Net margin and asset turnover were unchanged. The increase is most likely due to:
questions.explanation: With margin and turnover unchanged in the 3-step model, only leverage can explain the rise (12% × 1.25 = 15%). A lower tax rate would show up in net margin, which is unchanged.

questions.stem: NI is $150, EBT $200, EBIT $250, revenue $2,000, average total assets $1,600 and average equity $800. Which DuPont component is shown correctly?
Revenue is $7,300 and average receivables are $900. DSO is closest to:
questions.explanation: Receivables turnover = 7,300 ÷ 900 = 8.11; DSO = 365 ÷ 8.11 = **45 days**. 8.1 is the turnover.

questions.stem: Which change would most likely decrease a company's current ratio if it is currently 2.0?
options: Selling inventory at a profit for cash
questions.explanation: Buying inventory on credit adds equally to CA and CL, which lowers a ratio above 1 (e.g. 200/100 → 210/110 = 1.91). Collecting receivables leaves CA unchanged; selling at a profit raises CA.

questions.stem: Compared with peers, a company has higher asset turnover but lower net margin with the same ROE and leverage. This pattern best fits a:
questions.explanation: High turnover with low margin is a volume (discounter) model; premium pricing gives high margins and low turnover. Leverage is the same by assumption.

questions.stem: Which ratio is most appropriate for assessing a bank, rather than a manufacturer?
questions.explanation: Industry-specific ratios: banks are judged on capital adequacy, liquidity coverage and net interest margin. Inventory and fixed asset turnover suit manufacturers.

questions.stem: A company's DOH rose from 50 to 65 days while DSO and DPO were unchanged. Its cash conversion cycle:
questions.explanation: CCC = DSO + DOH − DPO; a 15-day rise in DOH lengthens the CCC by **15 days**, tying up more cash in working capital.

flashcards.back: DSO + DOH − DPO.
Purchases (= COGS + ending inventory − beginning inventory) ÷ avg AP gives payables turnover; DPO = 365 ÷ turnover.
(EBIT + lease payments) ÷ (interest + lease payments).
ROE = net margin × asset turnover × financial leverage.
ROE = tax burden (NI/EBT) × interest burden (EBT/EBIT) × EBIT margin × asset turnover × leverage.
g = retention rate × ROE = (1 − payout) × ROE.
(Cash + ST securities + receivables) ÷ daily cash expenditures.

modules.title: Introduction to Financial Statement Modeling
modules.summary: Building a sales-driven pro forma model, forecasting costs, working capital and capex, the effect of competition and inflation, choosing the forecast horizon, and behavioural biases that distort forecasts.

acca.note: MA/PM gave you budgeting and forecasting, and SBL gave you Porter's five forces. New for CFA: an analyst's sales-based pro forma model linked to ratios (DSO, DOH, capex/sales), inflation pass-through analysis and named behavioural biases in forecasting.

lessons.title: Building a sales-based pro forma model

cards.title: Start with revenue
cards.body:
Most models are **sales-driven**: forecast revenue, then tie costs, working capital and capex to it.

Revenue approaches: top-down (market size × share, GDP links), bottom-up (segments, volume × price, stores × sales per store), or hybrid.

Volume +5% and price +3% on revenue of 1,000 → 1,000 × 1.05 × 1.03 = **1,081.5**.

cards.title: Costs and the income statement
cards.body:
- **COGS**: via gross margin (watch input costs and pricing power)
- **SG&A**: split fixed vs variable; fixed costs create operating leverage
- **Interest**: rate × average debt
- **Tax**: effective rate, adjusted for one-offs

Example: revenue 2,200; gross margin 35% → gross profit 770; variable SG&A 12% (264) and fixed SG&A 50 → EBIT = **456**.

cards.title: Working capital and capex
cards.formula:
AR = revenue × DSO ÷ 365
Inventory = COGS × DOH ÷ 365
AP = purchases (or COGS) × DPO ÷ 365
where: often maintenance (≈ depreciation) + growth capex tied to sales

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: MA budgets were for **managers** with inside data. CFA models are built from **public** data: past ratios, management guidance and industry data. The forecast balance sheet must balance: cash or revolving debt is usually the plug.

cards.title: Porter's five forces in a model
cards.body:
Rivalry, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, buyer power and supplier power shape **pricing power** and margins.

Strong position (low rivalry, high barriers) → margins can be held or expanded in the forecast. Weak position → assume margin pressure and slower pass-through of cost increases.

cards.title: Inflation pass-through
cards.body:
Revenue 1,000; COGS 600 (gross margin 40%). Input costs rise 10% → COGS 660.

Pass on the **cost increase in dollars** (price +6%): revenue 1,060, gross profit stays 400 but margin falls to **37.7%**.
Raise price **10%**: revenue 1,100, gross profit 440, margin stays **40%**.

Pricing power decides which happens; volume may also fall if prices rise.

cards.title: Choosing the explicit horizon
cards.body:
Forecast explicitly until the company reaches a **steady state** (mature growth and margins), then use a terminal value.

Factors: business cycle length, investment strategy, company life cycle stage, and the investor's holding period. A cyclical firm needs at least a full cycle; a firm just after a big acquisition may need longer.

cards.title: Behavioural biases in forecasting
rows: Believing more data or complex models give control over outcomes
Slow to update for new information (anchoring on old view)
Extrapolating from a similar-looking case or recent trend
Seeking only evidence that supports the view

questions.stem: Forecast revenue is $1,095 and the company's DSO is expected to be 40 days. Forecast accounts receivable are:
questions.explanation: AR = 1,095 × 40 ÷ 365 = **$120**. $135 uses 45 days; $27 divides revenue by 40.

questions.stem: Current revenue is $1,000. The analyst expects volume growth of 5% and price increases of 3%. Next year's revenue forecast is closest to:
Revenue is forecast at $2,200 with a 35% gross margin. SG&A is 12% of revenue plus $50 fixed. Forecast EBIT is closest to:
questions.explanation: Gross profit = 770; SG&A = 264 + 50 = 314; EBIT = 770 − 314 = **$456**. $506 omits fixed SG&A; $770 is gross profit.

questions.stem: An analyst forecasts revenue by multiplying the expected number of stores by sales per store. This is a:
questions.explanation: Building revenue from company-level drivers (stores × sales per store) is **bottom-up**. Top-down starts from the economy or market size.

questions.stem: Revenue is $1,000 and COGS $600. Input costs rise 10% and the company raises prices just enough to pass on the dollar increase in costs. Its gross margin becomes closest to:
questions.explanation: COGS = 660; revenue = 1,060; gross profit 400 ÷ 1,060 = **37.7%**. Margin stays at 40% only if prices rise by the full 10%; 34.0% assumes no price increase (340 ÷ 1,000).

questions.stem: An analyst consistently produces very narrow ranges for forecast revenue and is often surprised by outcomes. This most likely reflects:
questions.explanation: Too-narrow ranges are a hallmark of **overconfidence**. Conservatism is slow updating; confirmation is seeking supporting evidence.

questions.stem: An analyst fails to revise forecasts adequately after a company announces a major new contract. This is best described as:
questions.explanation: Holding onto prior forecasts despite new information is **conservatism** bias.

questions.stem: For a highly cyclical company, the explicit forecast horizon should most likely:
options: match the industry's average debt maturity
cover at least a full business cycle
questions.explanation: A forecast should capture a normalised, full-cycle picture before a terminal value is applied.

questions.stem: Which factor would most likely support forecasting stable gross margins despite rising input costs?
options: Low threat of substitutes and high barriers to entry
Intense rivalry among many similar competitors
questions.explanation: Low substitution threat and high entry barriers give pricing power to pass on costs. Strong buyers and intense rivalry limit pass-through.

questions.stem: Forecast COGS is $1,460 and the company's expected days of inventory on hand is 50. Forecast inventory is closest to:
An analyst who searches mainly for data supporting her buy recommendation and dismisses negative reports is exhibiting:
questions.explanation: Seeking supporting evidence and discounting contrary evidence is **confirmation** bias.

questions.stem: In a pro forma balance sheet, which item is most commonly used as the balancing (plug) figure?
questions.explanation: Cash (or short-term borrowing/revolver) absorbs any surplus or shortfall so the balance sheet balances. PP&E and receivables are driven by capex and DSO assumptions.

questions.stem: A company with high fixed costs grows revenue 10%. Compared with a firm with mostly variable costs, its operating income will most likely grow:
questions.explanation: High fixed costs mean high **operating leverage**: operating income grows faster than revenue when sales rise.

flashcards.back: AR = revenue × DSO ÷ 365.
Inventory = COGS × DOH ÷ 365.
Top-down: economy/market size × share. Bottom-up: company drivers (volume × price, stores × sales per store).
Until steady state; at least a full cycle for cyclical firms; consider life cycle, strategy, holding period.
Overconfidence, illusion of control, conservatism, representativeness, confirmation.
Passing on only the dollar cost increase keeps gross profit but lowers gross margin %; pricing power (Porter's forces) determines pass-through.
